title: Lesion Overlap Ranks PET Segmentation Models but Does Not Certify Patient-Level Tumor Burden
abstract: Metabolic tumor volume (MTV) summarizes whole-body PET disease burden for prognostic stratification and treatment assessment. Automated MTV is useful only if its estimate is reliable for the individual patient, yet segmentation models are usually evaluated with overlap metrics such as Dice rather than burden error. We examined whether overlap metrics identify unreliable MTV estimates using 1,014 autoPET FDG PET/CT studies. We evaluated LesionTracer predictions held out from fine-tuning, compared five selected released models on 489 tumor-positive patients, and examined the findings in 597 PSMA studies. Across the five FDG models, ranking by higher mean Dice gave the same order as ranking by lower mean relative MTV error ($ρ=-1.00$, exact $p=0.017$). At the patient level, however, out-of-fold Dice tracked relative MTV error strongly ($ρ=-0.75$), yet 82 of 489 patients (16.8\%) fell on opposite sides of the Dice 0.80 and MTV-error 25\% thresholds. Within the training-exposed released models, correlations ranged from $-0.47$ to $-0.74$ over narrower, high-Dice ranges. Out of fold, opposing false-positive and false-negative volumes cancelled about one third of spatial error in net MTV. In 236 of 489 patients, each of the five models missed at least one lesion, though not necessarily the same lesion. Thus, agreement in average model rankings did not establish the reliability of individual MTV estimates or reveal shared lesion misses. PET segmentation benchmarks should report patient-level MTV error and missed-lesion counts alongside Dice and other overlap metrics.

title: CAPTOR: text-encoder-free grounding by counting caption co-occurrence over the visual words of a frozen encoder
abstract: Grounding a text query in an image needs a matrix scoring every term against every patch. Vision-language models compute it with an aligned text encoder, which many image encoders, such as histopathology-related models trained on slides alone, lack. The Caption-Anchored Patch-Term Occurrence Representation (CAPTOR) estimates the matrix without a text encoder. It clusters a frozen image encoder's patch tokens into visual words and describes each captioned image by its share of patches in each word. A term signature is the standardized difference of those shares between images whose captions mention the term and the rest. The matrix factorizes into a term-by-word table and a query-independent image factor, so an image is encoded once and a new term adds one table row. Against every training-free baseline, CAPTOR leads on Common Objects in Context (COCO), Pascal Visual Object Classes (VOC) and Cityscapes. On COCO, scored on the cells one object owns, it reaches 0.565 mean intersection over union (mIoU) against 0.502. On all three, it is also level with a text alignment trained on the same backbone, which needs gradients, a text encoder and several times the captions. On held-out breast-cancer slides, it exceeds the strongest baseline scoring patches with a pathology text encoder by 0.160 mIoU. Read through CAPTOR, UNI, an encoder trained on slides alone, exceeds such baselines by 0.132 on a common grid. Counting can therefore give a text interface to any image encoder trained without language, wherever captioned images exist.

title: Anchored Slice Propagation with Boundary Transport for 3D CT Segmentation from Three Orthogonal Annotated Slices
abstract: Sli2Vol propagates a binary mask through affinities between adjacent slices, but an error can persist because each prediction becomes the input to the next step. Three orthogonal annotations reduce dependence on any one chain, yet they offer more than three starting masks: where a chain crosses another annotated plane, the correct label is already known. Those labels could correct drift during propagation and indicate how much to trust each chain at fusion. Between annotated planes, the information carried by the chain may matter as well. A binary mask records foreground membership but discards distance to the boundary, a cue that could help follow gradual shape changes between slices.We address these two sources of error with a fixed pretrained affinity backbone. We anchor each chain by correcting its prediction where it crosses another annotated plane, then use its agreement with those labels to weight fusion. We compare this anchored mask with two ways of transporting boundary geometry: a truncated signed-distance field (SDF) propagated by dense affinity averaging, and a contour whose vertices follow motion cues from the same affinity. The contour tracker starts from a hand-crafted rule and learns a motion correction from supervoxel pseudo-objects in 506 CT volumes, without manual organ labels. On 2,091 held-out structure instances from approximately 403 CT scans spanning 17 abdominal structures, anchoring raises mean Dice from 0.737 with orthogonal mask propagation to 0.769 and improves every structure. Beyond the anchored mask, learned contour tracking improves Dice by 5.7\% for the esophagus and 5.9\% for the postcava, while SDF transport improves right-adrenal Dice by 2.8\%. The anchored methods have similar mean Dice (0.769--0.772); contour tracking performs worse on the kidneys, stomach, and hepatic vessel tree.

title: Mitigating Spurious Invariance in Contrastive Learning: A Probabilistic Self-Supervised Learning Framework for Medical Image Analysis
abstract: Owing to the prohibitive cost of manual annotation for enormous medical images, self-supervised learning (SSL) has gained substantial attention and shown promise in various medical imaging tasks. Among SSL approaches, contrastive learning has emerged as a prominent one, encouraging models to encode semantic information that remains invariant between different augmented views. However, this invariance can be spurious for medical images, as subtle but critical medical features can be suppressed during augmentations. In this paper, we mitigate this issue by encoding the learned feature embeddings as probability distributions rather than fixed vectors, thus capturing a richer and more nuanced spectrum of information. Furthermore, we propose a unified probabilistic framework that seamlessly integrates multiple SSL approaches. Our method achieves superior performance over the state-of-the-art SSL methods on various downstream tasks across multiple datasets, including medical image segmentation and classification. We further validate the method through additional analyses of robustness to stronger augmentations, label efficiency under limited fine-tuning labels, and computational trade-offs. The code is released at https://github.com/wwzjer/ProbSSL.

title: ME^2FDiff: Multiscale Expert Enhancing Feature Diffusion in Residual Network for Brain Tumor Segmentation
abstract: Automated segmentation of post-treatment glioma from MRI is essential for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning, yet remains difficult. Surgery and chemoradiotherapy cause structural changes in brain like resection cavities, edema, and fibrosis, that alter imaging appearance and mimic tumor recurrence. Contemporary segmentation architectures attain high accuracy with two limitations. First, the bottleneck originates from the deepest encoder stage, so one representation must serve sub-regions that differ widely in size and appearance. Second, they produce the segmentation in a single forward pass with no mechanism for refinement. We propose ME^2FDiff, a single-model architecture, addressing both. An attention-conditioned spectral diffusion block refines the bottleneck. It uses the image-conditioned latent diffusion process with two processes: a spatial pre-attention gate and a spectral fusion block whose timestep-adaptive bandpass filter selects the informative frequency band at each noise level. A multiscale expert-enhanced feature block fuses the intermediate encoder scales into the bottleneck through expert-selected shared tokens, guaranteeing balanced utilization without an auxiliary loss. On the BraTS 2024 post-treatment glioma dataset, ME^2FDiff achieves the best results on every tumor sub-region among all single-model baselines (91.23% Dice, 84.52% IOU, 2.13 mm HD95 on whole-tumor) and surpasses a three-expert ensemble on both overlap metrics at roughly one-third of its inference cost. Against recent state-of-the-art methods retrained under identical conditions, it maintains the strongest performance with the fewest parameters of any competing model. These findings demonstrate that a single, compact network can absorb the specialization, usually sought through ensembling or larger architectures.

title: Diagnosis and Management of Acute Cholangitis: A Review.
abstract: Acute cholangitis (AC) is a potentially fatal biliary tract infection most commonly caused by gallstones. While modern-day treatments with antibiotics and biliary decompression have drastically decreased mortality rates, AC still requires prompt intervention. Diagnosis of AC traditionally relied on the presence of the Charcot triad, which has since proven to incompletely capture the complexity of this condition. Modern-day diagnosis, severity grading, and management guidelines provide a more holistic approach. Tokyo Guidelines (TG) are widely used, though newer guidelines, namely the BILE criteria, have recently emerged. These criteria include demonstration of inflammation, cholestasis, and biliary obstruction. Ultrasound is first-line imaging modality with computed tomography or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography often used for diagnostic dilemmas. Treatment is dependent on severity, though guidelines generally recommend early decompression (most commonly with endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography [ERCP]) for moderate to severe cases. The optimal timing of biliary drainage remains unclear, with mixed evidence from observational studies and no universal definition of what constitutes "early" vs "urgent" drainage. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy should be performed during index hospitalization, when possible, with multiple studies demonstrating lower morbidity and mortality rates when compared with interval procedures. The prognosis of AC is favorable if treated swiftly and appropriately; in turn, mortality rates increase with severity and delays in diagnosis. AC can be challenging to diagnose and the precise timing of biliary drainage and cholecystectomy is debated. This comprehensive review reflects the most recent evidence and recommendations on severity grading, resuscitation, and timing of ERCP and cholecystectomy to assist clinicians who manage these complex patients.

title: Diagnostic image quality of shoulder magnetic resonance imaging at 0.55T in healthy subjects and patients with rotator cuff injury: Prospective comparison with 1.5T.
abstract: Background Lower‑field 0.55 T MRI scanners with large‑bore design could offer patients more comfortable feeling and flexible position. With the advances in deep‑learning reconstruction and hardware optimization, 0.55T have greatly improved their image quality and cost‑effectiveness for musculoskeletal applications. However, its feasibility for shoulder evaluation remains unstudied. Purpose To evaluate the image quality of shoulder using 0.55T MRI in volunteers and patients with rotator cuff injury with comparison of conventional 1.5T. Methods Fifty participants (25 volunteers, 25 patients) were prospectively enrolled. All participants underwent shoulder MRI both at open 0.55T with contour coils and deep learning (DL) and 1.5T MR without DL. The nonparametric method was utilized to compare image quality scores and quantitative metrics (signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (|CNR|)). Arthroscopy have been conducted in 16 patients. Kappa statistics was used to assess interobserver and interstudy agreement for lesion evaluation. Comfort feeling was also compared. Results The scan time was 11'25″ for 0.55T MRI and 11'42″ for 1.5T MRI. The interobserver analyses showed high consistency (κ = 0.771-1.000, P: 0.008 ∼ < 0.001) among 3 readers. The scores for coronal fat suppressed T2 weighted imaging (fsT2WI) and coronal T1 weighted imaging (T1WI) were significantly higher for 0.55T MRI. Most sequences at 0.55T demonstrated significantly higher SNRs (P:0.04 ∼ < 0.001). Additionally, |CNR| values for lesions were significantly higher in fs proton weighted imaging (PDWI) and fsT2WI at 0.55T. Perfect interstudy agreement between 0.55T and 1.5T was observed between 2 readers (Kappa = 1, P < 0.001) for lesion assessment. Agreement between MRI findings and arthroscopic results was perfect or good. The 0.55T system received higher scores in comfort ratings. Conclusion The 0.55T MRI with DL, showed comparable or better image quality in healthy subjects and patients with rotator cuff injury to 1.5T MRI without DL.

title: Microwave-Responsive AIE Nanocomposite Induces Immunogenic Senescence for Imaging-Guided Therapy and Bone Repair in Osteosarcoma.
abstract: Osteosarcoma remains challenging due to incomplete tumor resection, local recurrence, and limited immunostimulatory efficacy of current microwave (MW)-based therapies. Here, we develop a multifunctional theranostic nanoplatform, GPC3@TTBC, by conjugating an osteosarcoma-targeting anti-GPC3 peptide onto aggregation-induced emission (AIE) nanoparticles. GPC3@TTBC enables selective tumor accumulation and high-contrast near-infrared fluorescence imaging, allowing precise tumor margin delineation and superior tumor-to-background resolution compared with clinically used dyes, including effective visualization in patient-derived xenograft models. Upon MW irradiation, lysosome-localized GPC3@TTBC generates robust nonthermal reactive oxygen species (ROS) through enhanced charge separation and electron transfer, resulting in substantial tumor cell apoptosis while simultaneously inducing a prominent immunogenic senescence-associated phenotype and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) response. Importantly, MW + GPC3@TTBC suppressed tumor cell migration and invasion in vitro and reduced pulmonary metastatic lesions in vivo. Meanwhile, the SASP promoted dendritic cell maturation and cytotoxic T lymphocyte activation, thereby enhancing antitumor immune responses and remodeling the tumor immune microenvironment. Beyond tumor eradication, GPC3@TTBC facilitates osteogenic microenvironment reconstruction and bone regeneration after tumor clearance, while exhibiting favorable biosafety. Collectively, GPC3@TTBC integrates targeted fluorescence-guided imaging, MW-enhanced ROS generation, immunogenic senescence induction, and bone regeneration, providing a comprehensive theranostic strategy for precise osteosarcoma treatment.

title: A CT Lesion Foundation Model for Non-Invasive Assessment of Hepatocellular Carcinoma Aggressiveness and Prediction of Recurrence Risk.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with high recurrence rates following curative resection. Accurate non-invasive assessment of tumor aggressiveness and recurrence risk is critical for surgical decision-making and postoperative surveillance, yet remains challenging with conventional imaging modalities. Here, we developed a CT lesion foundation model (LFM), trained via self-supervised learning on 32,120 generic lesion and 6,387 HCC-specific CT patches to capture transferable intra-lesional imaging phenotypes. Across one internal and two external validation cohorts, the sequentially pretrained LFM (LFM-Seq) achieved area under the curve values of 0.916, 0.846, and 0.920 for microvascular invasion (MVI) assessment, and 0.833, 0.885 and 0.795 for pathological grade assessment. The model remained robust under scenarios of limited training data and tumor localization perturbations. Furthermore, LFM-Seq-derived risk scores stratified recurrence-free survival (RFS), yielding an externally validated C-index of 0.701, and remained independently associated with RFS after adjusting for clinicopathological factors. Exploratory biological interpretability analyses showed that LFM-Seq-derived risk phenotypes were associated with suppressed lymphocyte-related immune programs. These results suggest that CT lesion foundation models can support non-invasive and robust characterization of HCC aggressiveness, recurrence risk stratification and discovery of interpretable prognostic imaging biomarkers.

title: 18 F-FGln PET/CT Imaging of Glutamine Uptake Has Potential for Predicting Immunotherapy Response in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: We investigated whether glutamine (Gln) uptake, imaged by 18 F-(2S,4R)-4-fluoroglutamine ( 18 F-FGln) PET/CT, could predict and modulate immunotherapy response in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Analysis of the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)-Liver Hepatocellular Carcinoma (LIHC) dataset revealed that SLC1A5 expression-which encodes a primary Gln uptake channel in HCC cells-was significantly associated with poor prognosis, higher tumor grade, and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. In murine HCC models, tumors with high 18 F-FGln uptake exhibited elevated Slc1a5 expression and poor response to anti-PD-1 therapy, whereas low-uptake tumors were more sensitive to immunotherapy. Genetic knockdown of Slc1a5 reduced 18 F-FGln uptake, enhanced anti-PD-1 efficacy, increased cytotoxic T lymphocyte infiltration, and decreased regulatory T cell abundance. Transcriptomic and single-cell analyses revealed activation of antitumor immune pathways and reprogramming toward an immune-inflamed phenotype after Slc1a5 suppression. V-9302 decreased tumor Gln uptake, as measured by 18 F-FGln PET/CT, and sensitized HCC to PD-1 blockade. In patient-derived organoid-T cell co-culture systems, low-SLC1A5 organoids were susceptible to PD-1 blockade, whereas high-SLC1A5 organoids were resistant, consistent with 18 F-FGln PET/CT findings. These results identify Gln uptake as a checkpoint of immune evasion in HCC and support that 18 F-FGln PET/CT has the potential to predict and monitor immunotherapy response.

title: The Prenatal Phenotype: Illustrating the Complexities of Genetic Testing and Interpretation With the Goal of Understanding the Fetal Presentation of Genetic Disease.
abstract: Advanced prenatal imaging and chromosomal microarray have improved detection of fetal anomalies, yet many structurally abnormal fetuses remain without a unifying diagnosis. This manuscript describes representative prenatal cases evaluated with genome sequencing (GS) or exome sequencing (ES), demonstrating how genomic data refine etiologic understanding, reshape counseling, and reveal the complexities of variant interpretation within the prenatal context. Three illustrative fetal cases were selected based on characteristic imaging findings, including short long bones, echogenic kidneys, multisystem anomalies, and severe limb reduction defects. All underwent detailed ultrasound, standard genetic evaluation, and ultimately GS or ES. Variants were classified using ACMG/AMP criteria with prenatal-specific interpretive considerations. Diagnoses included a 17q12 deletion with concomitant ARID1B-related Coffin-Siris syndrome, a de novo FRYL variant in the setting of multisystem anomalies, and a de novo KMT2E truncating variant identified alongside placental pathology supportive of treated leptospirosis. Findings alter recurrence risks, reveal dual diagnoses, and highlight prognostic complexities. Prenatal sequencing clarifies fetal diagnoses, informs reproductive planning, and refines risk counseling, yet interpretation is constrained by limited prenatal phenotyping and reliance on postnatal genotype-phenotype literature. Integration of GS/ES with imaging and multidisciplinary counseling is essential as sequencing becomes routine in perinatal care.

title: Anatomical and histological characterization of the heart of the scarlet ibis (Eudocimus ruber).
abstract: Detailed information on the cardiac morphology of the scarlet ibis (Eudocimus ruber) remains limited. This study aimed to characterize the gross and microscopic anatomy of this species' heart and provide morphometric data. We examined six specimens (three males and three females) using gross anatomical analysis, morphometry, conventional radiography, three-dimensional scanning, light microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. The mean heart mass was 5.93 ± 1.49 g (n = 6), corresponding to 1.10 ± 0.23% of body mass, and the mean radiographic cardiothoracic ratio was 66.90 ± 5.78% (n = 3). Macroscopic examination identified three venae cavae: the right and left cranial venae cavae and the caudal vena cava. The left atrioventricular valve had two cusps with chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, whereas the right atrioventricular valve had a single muscular fold. Histological examination identified uninucleated and binucleated Purkinje fibers in the subendocardial region, extending into myocardial muscle bundles. The base of the aorta showed hyaline cartilage containing chondrocytes and chondroblasts, with no bone tissue identified in the examined sections. These findings provide anatomical, morphometric, and histological data on the heart of E. ruber and a basis for future comparative studies of avian cardiac morphology.

title: Inferior Patient-Reported Outcomes After Primary Hip Arthroscopy in the Congenitally Narrow Joint Despite Similar Cartilage Quality When Compared With a Propensity-Matched Control Group.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the outcomes after hip arthroscopy in patients with a symmetric congenitally narrowed hip joint space without radiographic evidence of degenerative changes. Methods Consecutive patients with Tönnis grade 0 undergoing hip arthroscopy between 2009 and 2022 for femoroacetabular impingement syndrome with labral repair and minimum 2-year postoperative outcomes were eligible for inclusion in the study. Subjects were considered congenitally narrowed if they had an average bilateral joint space width less than 3 mm without other radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis. This cohort was propensity-matched to patients with an average joint space greater than 4 mm. Preoperative demographic and radiographic variables, intraoperative findings and procedures, and postoperative outcomes were compared between the 2 groups. Results Thirty-one patients in the congenitally narrow group were propensity-matched to 57 patients in the control cohort. The groups were comparable in age, gender, body mass index, and radiographic variables other than joint space width between cohorts. The congenitally narrow group had no differences in femoral head or acetabular chondral damage compared with the control cohort (P > .05 for both). There were significantly lower postoperative patient-reported outcomes in the congenitally narrow group across multiple patient reported outcome measures. At 5-year time point, the control group had a significantly higher percentage, meeting patient acceptable symptomatic state for modified Harris Hip Score (80% vs 52%, P = .01) and International Hip Outcome Tool-12 (80% vs 56%, P = .03) and minimal clinically important difference for modified Harris Hip Score (89.5% vs 63%). There was no difference in revision arthroscopy (9.7% vs 10.5%, P = .9) or arthroplasty-free survivorship (100% vs 96.5%; P = .29) between the congenitally narrow and control groups, respectively. Conclusions There were no differences in intraoperative cartilage quality or reoperation rate in patients with a congenitally narrow joint compared with a propensity-matched control cohort. However, despite the lack of radiographic osteoarthritis, patients with a congenitally narrow joint had inferior patient-reported outcomes scores compared with the study control group. Level of evidence Level III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Open-Source and Commercial 3-Dimensional Computed Tomography Methods Show Limited Agreement for Classifying Acetabular Morphology in Patients Undergoing Hip Arthroscopy.
abstract: Purpose To compare acetabular morphology classifications derived from a validated open-source (freely available) method with those derived from commercially available software in patients undergoing hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement syndrome. Methods We analyzed preoperative 3-dimensional computed tomography imaging in patients with femoroacetabular impingement syndrome using open-source and commercial software. The open-source method calculated acetabular coverage across 5 regions and generated z -scores relative to an internal normative database. Hips with z -scores ≥2 or ≤-2 were classified as abnormal. The commercial method categorized hips as normal, undercovered, or overcovered based on published thresholds (lateral center-edge angle, Tönnis angle, coverage percentage, and crossover sign) and focal depth mapping. The primary outcome was categorical agreement between methods. Results Seventy-six hips (55 women, 21 men; mean age 35.5 ± 12.3 years) were included. The open-source method classified 58/76 hips as normal, 10/76 as dysplastic, and 8/76 as overcovered. The commercial method classified 14/76 hips as normal, 29/76 as undercovered, and 33/76 as overcovered. A total of 23/76 hips were classified the same in both systems and called agreed. Disagreements (53/76 hips) fell into 3 categories: (1) essentially similar despite different labels because of borderline z -scores or small focal areas (n = 24), (2) disagreements driven by Tönnis angle alone (n = 8), and (3) true disagreements (n = 21). Notably, 5 hips (6.6%) showed opposite classifications (e.g., dysplastic vs overcovered). Subanalysis of z -scores showed that 69.8% of disagreements reflected borderline morphology ( z -scores of ±1-2). Conclusions Although both open-source and commercial methods provide 3-dimensional classification of acetabular morphology, categorical agreement was limited. Most disagreements reflected borderline morphology or small focal areas of uncertain clinical relevance. A minority showed true classification opposites. Clinical relevance Awareness of the methodological differences between open-source and commercial 3-dimensional computed tomography platforms may help surgeons appropriately interpret acetabular morphology classifications during preoperative planning for patients undergoing hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement syndrome.

title: Pelvic sleeve pyeloplasty in adults: A technical refinement of Anderson-Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty.
abstract: Objectives To describe pelvic sleeve pyeloplasty, a technical refinement of Anderson-Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty for adult ureteropelvic junction obstruction, and to report perioperative and functional outcomes in an initial adult series. Methods Between 2009 and 2018, 12 adult patients with symptomatic ureteropelvic junction obstruction underwent pelvic sleeve pyeloplasty using a transperitoneal laparoscopic or robot-assisted approach. Preoperative evaluation included computed tomography intravenous pyelography and diuretic Tc-99m MAG3 renography. Patients with previous failed ureteropelvic junction surgery were excluded. The technique preserves and incorporates a sleeve of renal pelvic tissue into the reconstruction to create a broad, continuous, tension-free ureteropelvic anastomosis while minimizing manipulation of healthy ureteric tissue. Results All procedures were completed successfully without conversion to open surgery. Eight patients underwent laparoscopic and four underwent robot-assisted pyeloplasty. Mean operative time was 185 min (range 160-255 min), and estimated blood loss ranged from 90 to 350 mL. One patient had intraoperative bleeding from a gonadal vein injury, controlled without transfusion. One patient developed a transient postoperative febrile episode (Clavien-Dindo grade II). No patient developed urinary leakage or required secondary intervention. At a mean follow-up of 38 months (range 24-50 months), all patients were asymptomatic and diuretic Tc-99m MAG3 renography demonstrated unobstructed drainage. Conclusions Pelvic sleeve pyeloplasty is a feasible modification of dismembered pyeloplasty that preserves ureteric length, minimizes ureteric manipulation and facilitates a wide, continuous, tension-free ureteropelvic anastomosis. Larger comparative studies are required to validate reproducibility and long-term efficacy.

title: Targeting Ninjurin-1-Mediated Microglial Pyroptosis Attenuates Neuroinflammation and Neuronal Injury Following Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
abstract: Objective This study aims to delineate the pathophysiological contribution of Ninjurin-1 (Ninj1) to secondary neural injury following intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), specifically elucidating its function in microglial pyroptosis and its upstream transcriptional governance by nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB). Methods Candidate targets were initially identified via in silico transcriptomic profiling. We subsequently employed a collagenase-induced murine ICH paradigm alongside hemin-challenged microglia. Mechanistic pathways were interrogated utilizing targeted genetic silencing (in vivo siRNA and in vitro shRNA) and pharmacological blockade. Disease phenotypes-encompassing pyroptotic execution, neuroinflammation, and collateral neuronal death-were quantified via immunoblotting, molecular assays, and histopathology. The upstream regulatory architecture was validated through ChIP-qPCR, EMSA, and dual-luciferase reporter assays. Results Bioinformatic screening highlighted Ninj1 as a prominently upregulated candidate transcript post-ICH, a finding corroborated by robust induction in both in vivo and in vitro hemorrhagic models. Through prophylactic in vivo target validation, Ninj1 depletion restricted perihematomal edema and preserved sensorimotor function. Mechanistically, suppressing Ninj1 abrogated the microglial pyroptotic cascade and mitigated collateral neurotoxicity. Furthermore, NF-κB was shown to transcriptionally activate NLRP3 and Ninj1, although direct promoter enrichment in the ChIP-qPCR assay was statistically significant only for the Nlrp3 locus. Conclusions Ninj1 functions as a terminal executioner of microglial pyroptosis and a critical amplifier of post-ICH neuroinflammation. Governed by a coordinated NF-κB-dependent transcriptional program alongside NLRP3, this signaling axis exacerbates secondary brain injury, positioning Ninj1 as a viable molecular candidate for neuroprotective target validation.

title: Association of High-Grade Components < 20% on DFS in Stage I Lung Adenocarcinoma: A Real-World Study of Risk Analysis and Predictive Nomogram Development.
abstract: Objective To assess whether high-grade components occupying < 20% of the tumor have prognostic value and whether an Adjusted Grade nomogram improves risk stratification in Stage I invasive lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). Methods We retrospectively analyzed 1539 patients with pathologically confirmed Stage I invasive LUAD undergoing R0 resection; 1321 with follow-up, including 967 with preoperative CT. Tumors were classified by IASLC Grade and reclassified according to predominant pattern and high-grade components; Adjusted Grade 3 was subdivided into MHGC ≤ 5%, DHGC > 5% to < 20%, and SHGC ≥ 20%. Cox models identified DFS predictors. Nomograms were internally validated with 1000 bootstrap resamples and assessed for discrimination, calibration, and net benefit. Results During a median 38-month follow-up, 124 DFS events occurred. Adjusted Grade 3 independently predicted recurrence (HR 3.07, 95% CI 1.54-6.12), while MHGC and DHGC were associated with poorer DFS (HR 3.95, 95% CI 1.53-10.15; HR 2.55, 95% CI 1.12-5.80). In the CT subgroup, consolidation-to-tumor ratio (CTR) independently predicted DFS (HR 3.08, 95% CI 1.46-6.51). Optimism-corrected C-index was 0.740 for the Adjusted Grade-based nomogram, compared with 0.727 for the IASLC-based nomogram and 0.612 for TNM staging. After adding CTR, they were 0.763 and 0.745 for the Adjusted Grade- and IASLC-based nomogram. Decision-curve analysis showed similar net benefit profiles for the two nomograms. Conclusion High-grade components below 20% were associated with poorer DFS. The Adjusted Grade-based nomogram improved internal discrimination versus IASLC Grade and TNM staging but showed no clear clinical-benefit advantage over IASLC Grade. External validation is needed to establish optimal thresholds and clinical utility.

title: Guided bone regeneration using CAD-CAM zirconia barriers: A case series with digital evaluation of bone changes.
abstract: Background CAD/CAM zirconia barriers represent an advanced option for guided bone regeneration (GBR) in three-dimensional defects, integrating mechanical stability, biocompatibility, and digital precision. The objectives of this case series were to evaluate, clinically, histologically, and three-dimensionally, the use of customized zirconia barriers designed using CAD/CAM technology in GBR procedures. Methods and results Three patients with severe maxillary bone atrophy were included and treated with GBR using customized zirconia barriers. Digital planning was performed based on cone beam computed tomography and intraoral scanning, followed by CAD/CAM design and fabrication of the barriers. The defects were regenerated using a mixture of autogenous bone and xenograft. After the healing period, implants were placed using guided surgery, and bone biopsies were obtained for histological analysis. Bone gains were evaluated through linear and volumetric digital analysis based on three-dimensional model superimposition. All surgeries were completed without complications, allowing implant placement in all cases without the need for additional augmentation procedures. Mean horizontal bone gains of 6.17 mm at the crestal level and mean vertical gains of 2.62 mm were recorded, with maximum values of up to 5.11 mm. Volumetric analysis revealed bone gains of 797.158 mm 3 (case 1), 459.718 mm 3 (case 2), and 1416.870 mm 3 (case 3). Histological analysis demonstrated vital, well-vascularized newly formed bone undergoing active remodeling, with no evidence of inflammation. Conclusions Customized zirconia barriers demonstrated favorable clinical and histological outcomes in GBR. The digital workflow, combined with three-dimensional analysis, allowed a precise and reproducible evaluation of bone changes. Key points This case series presents a comprehensive clinical protocol for guided bone regeneration using customized zirconia barriers, based on prosthetically driven planning, individualized barrier design, graft stability, and meticulous peri-implant soft tissue management, including histological analysis of the regenerated tissue. The incorporation of a standardized digital protocol for linear and volumetric analysis enabled an objective, reproducible, and precise evaluation of dimensional changes in the alveolar ridge. Plain language summary Significant bone loss in the upper jaw can prevent dental implants from being placed in the correct position. In these situations, rebuilding the lost bone is necessary to achieve a stable long-term outcome. This case series describes the use of customized zirconia barriers designed to fit each bone defect and support bone regeneration. After the healing period, all treated defects showed sufficient bone gain to allow implant placement according to the original prosthetic treatment plan. Histological analysis confirmed the formation of new bone, while a standardized digital measurement protocol provided an objective and reproducible assessment of the bone changes achieved after treatment. These findings suggest that customized zirconia barriers may represent a promising alternative for the management of complex bone defects, although studies involving larger numbers of patients are needed to confirm these results.

title: Right Ventricular Dysfunction and Ventriculo-Arterial Uncoupling in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Phenotype-Specific Review of Mechanisms, Diagnosis, and Therapeutic Strategies.
abstract: Background Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) accounts for nearly half of all global heart failure cases. Historically viewed as a left-centric diastolic disorder, emerging evidence identifies right ventricular (RV) dysfunction and impaired ventriculo-arterial (RV-PA) coupling as central drivers of exercise intolerance, functional decline, and adverse clinical outcomes. Objectives This review synthesizes current evidence on the pathophysiological mechanisms, advanced diagnostic modalities, prognostic implications, and phenotype-specific therapies for RV dysfunction in HFpEF, advocating for a transition to systematic biventricular evaluation. Methods A structured, PRISMA-informed search of PubMed and Scopus (2015-2024) identified 74 eligible studies evaluating RV structure, function, and hemodynamics in HFpEF cohorts. Results RV dysfunction is prevalent in 19% to 33% of HFpEF patients and independently predicts all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalizations. Key pathophysiological drivers include post-capillary pulmonary hypertension, impaired RV lusitropy, systemic inflammation, and inter-ventricular dependence. Non-invasive markers notably speckle-tracking echocardiography, 4D-flow cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), and the TAPSE/PASP ratio enable early identification of subclinical RV-PA uncoupling. While traditional heart failure therapies show limited efficacy, emerging options including SGLT2 inhibitors, interatrial shunt devices, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and targeted pulmonary vasodilators demonstrate potential to preserve RV strain and restore hemodynamics across distinct clinical phenotypes. Conclusions RV dysfunction is a major prognostic marker in HFpEF. Routine inclusion of RV-PA coupling indices in diagnostic and risk-stratification algorithms is essential to guide precision-based, phenotype-guided management and improve clinical trajectories.

title: Automated Detection of Positioning Errors in Bitewing Radiographs Using Deep Learning.
abstract: Bitewing radiographs (BWs) are essential diagnostic tools in dentistry, but are often affected by positioning errors, compromising their diagnostic value and increasing retake rates. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a deep learning-based automated system for detecting and classifying BW type (premolar/molar), side (right/left), and common positioning errors in a controlled mannequin-based setting. A total of 403 BWs were collected from dental student assessments acquired from dental radiology mannequins. BWs were consensus-labeled by dentomaxillofacial radiology experts for type, side, and the most common positioning errors. A balanced data set supported training and validation. Convolutional neural network architectures, including ResNet and DenseNet variants, were trained from scratch and evaluated as independent classification tasks using stratified fivefold cross-validation. Performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and area under the curve, reported as mean ± standard deviation across folds. A confusion matrix was generated for multi-class cone-cutting error (CCE) severity classification. The system achieved accuracies of 95.8% for BW type classification, 99.0% for side classification, 96.3% for CCE detection, and 93.4% for interproximal overlap detection. Multi-class CCE classification achieved an accuracy of 79.3%, with reliable identification of "critical" and "minimal" errors. Detection of incorrect receptor placement achieved an accuracy of 73.2%. The CNN-based system showed strong performance for bitewing type, side, binary cone-cutting error, and interproximal overlap classification in mannequin-acquired radiographs. Performance was more limited for multi-class cone-cutting severity and incorrect receptor placement. These findings support the potential use of deep learning for radiographic quality assessment in education and quality-control workflows. A validation study using patient-acquired bitewing radiographs from clinical settings is required before clinical deployment.

title: Triphasic waves in leptomeningeal metastases and cycling alternating pattern of encephalopathy during sleep.
abstract: Background Triphasic waves (TWs), now termed generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology, may be mistaken for nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE), particularly in critically ill patients. Changes in vigilance over time can help distinguish encephalopathic patterns from ictal activity. Case presentation A 69-year-old woman with breast cancer and leptomeningeal metastases developed progressive mutism and impaired consciousness. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed atypical cells and markedly elevated protein, while brain MRI demonstrated bilateral sulcal hyperintensities, most prominent in the posterior regions. An EEG performed 1 week after bevacizumab and paclitaxel were discontinued showed only mild background slowing without epileptiform discharges. A repeat EEG 1 week later showed nearly continuous TWs. The discharges disappeared during spontaneous sleep and recurred periodically, consistent with a cyclic alternating pattern of encephalopathy during sleep (CAPE). In the absence of significant metabolic and toxic derangements, these features favored an encephalopathic rather than ictal pattern. Given the advanced disease and poor prognosis, care remained supportive and palliative. Conclusion This case highlights the importance of interpreting TWs within their clinical context and in relation to the state of vigilance. Their disappearance at sleep onset, with periodic recurrence during sleep producing a CAPE, supports an encephalopathic rather than ictal interpretation, helping to avoid misdiagnosis of NCSE and unnecessary administration of antiseizure medications.

title: Thymidine Kinase 2 Deficiency in the Era of Approved Therapy: From Diagnosis to Evidence Across the Disease Spectrum.
abstract: Thymidine kinase 2 deficiency (TK2d) is an ultra-rare autosomal recessive mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) maintenance disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the nuclear TK2 gene. Loss of TK2 activity disrupts intramitochondrial deoxynucleotide pools, impairing mtDNA replication and resulting in a spectrum of quantitative (mtDNA depletion) and qualitative (multiple deletions) alterations whose severity is a key determinant of prognosis. Clinically, TK2d presents as a continuous phenotypic spectrum, from rapidly progressive infantile disease to adult-onset forms, predominantly manifesting as progressive myopathy with early bulbar and respiratory involvement, the principal drivers of morbidity and mortality, with overall severity inversely correlated with age at onset. Central nervous system involvement may occur in severe early-onset cases, whilst extramuscular manifestations are otherwise limited, with sensorineural hearing loss and subclinical axonal sensory neuropathy described across the spectrum. Circulating biomarkers, particularly GDF-15, support diagnosis, correlate with disease severity and show dynamic changes with treatment; serum creatinine, muscle MRI fat fraction and forced vital capacity further contribute to prognostic stratification. Oral supplementation with doxecitine and doxribtimine, recently approved by the FDA (2025) and EMA (2026) for patients with symptom onset ≤ 12 years, represents the first disease-modifying therapy for TK2d, demonstrating marked survival benefit, stabilisation of disease progression and partial recovery of motor function. Evidence in adult patients remains limited and largely retrospective, underscoring the need for dedicated prospective studies with outcome measures sensitive to slowly progressive phenotypes.

Central nervous system involvement may occur in severe early-onset cases, whilst extramuscular manifestations are otherwise limited, with sensorineural hearing loss and subclinical axonal sensory neuropathy described across the spectrum. Circulating biomarkers, particularly GDF-15, support diagnosis, correlate with disease severity and show dynamic changes with treatment; serum creatinine, muscle MRI fat fraction and forced vital capacity further contribute to prognostic stratification. Evidence in adult patients remains limited and largely retrospective, underscoring the need for dedicated prospective studies with outcome measures sensitive to slowly progressive phenotypes.

title: Daytime Idle Energy Reduction in Radiotherapy Simulation Computed Tomography: A Prospective Workflow-Based Evaluation.
abstract: Introduction Previous computed tomography (CT) energy-saving studies have primarily focused on after-hours shutdown or idle energy use in diagnostic CT. Radiotherapy simulation, however, includes preparation and immobilisation steps that may prolong daytime non-acquisition periods. This study quantified daytime energy use in radiotherapy simulation CT and evaluated the contribution of power-saving operation. Methods In this prospective single-centre study, electrical power consumption was directly measured using a three-phase power logger during five baseline and five power-saving weekdays (08:00-18:00). Power measurements were integrated with patient in-room intervals and simulation procedure categories. Staff perceptions of workflow impact were assessed using an anonymous questionnaire, and carbon implications were estimated from the measured energy reduction. Results Mean directly measured clinical-hour energy consumption decreased from 38.7 to 36.5 kWh/day with power-saving operation, a 5.8% reduction. Non-acquisition time during patient presence varied markedly by procedure, from 56.5% for respiratory-gated four-dimensional CT to 97.1% for head-and-neck simulation. Power-saving operation shifted daytime power use towards a lower-power state, corresponding to an estimated reduction of 0.84-1.01 kg-CO 2 per clinical day across the emission-factor sensitivity range. Twenty of 21 staff (95.2%) reported no impact on patient throughput. Conclusion Power-saving operation reduced daytime energy consumption without meaningful workflow disruption. Radiotherapy simulation CT has prolonged, procedure-dependent idle periods arising from radiotherapy-specific preparation workflows, highlighting a practical and previously undercharacterised opportunity for energy reduction.

title: Pulmonary Vein Anatomy, Cooling Kinetics, and Recurrence After Cryoballoon Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation.
abstract: Background Cryoballoon pulmonary vein isolation depends on balloon-to-ostium contact. We assessed whether computed tomography-derived pulmonary vein ostial area (OA) and ovality index (OI) were associated with cooling after accounting for pulmonary vein (PV) branch and within-patient clustering, and whether PV anatomy was associated with recurrence. Methods We retrospectively studied 120 patients with symptomatic atrial fibrillation undergoing second-generation cryoballoon ablation. Vein-level associations with nadir temperature, 1 min temperature, and time to isolation were assessed using linear mixed-effects models with a patient random intercept and PV branch as a fixed effect; generalized estimating equations served as sensitivity analyses. Given 23 post-blanking recurrences, logistic models were limited to left atrial volume index (LAVI) and one clinically selected covariate, with Firth-penalized regression as a sensitivity analysis. Results All patients achieved acute PV isolation. Larger OA was associated with lower nadir temperature ( β = -0.583°C per 50 mm 2 ; 95% CI, -0.910 to -0.257; p < 0.001) and 1 min temperature ( β = -0.441°C per 50 mm 2 ; 95% CI, -0.764 to -0.118; p = 0.008) after branch and clustering adjustment. OI was not associated with either temperature outcome. Twenty-three patients (19.2%) developed recurrent atrial arrhythmia. LAVI was associated with recurrence (adjusted OR, 1.659 per 10 mL/m 2 ; 95% CI, 1.250-2.201; p < 0.001), whereas persistent AF was not. Conclusions OA showed a modest association with cryoballoon temperatures but should not be used as a stand-alone prognostic marker. LAVI remained associated with recurrence in parsimonious patient-level analyses.

title: Super-Resolution Ultrasound for Lymph Node Evaluation: Diagnostic Value of Static Time-Point Parameters Versus Dynamic Temporal Changes.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate quantitative super-resolution ultrasound (SRUS) parameters (static central-to-peripheral ratios and dynamic temporal changes) for differentiating benign and metastatic lymph nodes, and to compare the performance of corresponding predictive models. Methods A prospective study included 172 pathologically confirmed lymph nodes (100 benign, 72 metastatic). SRUS was performed to derive density and velocity parameters, with central-to-peripheral ratios and temporal changes calculated. Static and dynamic models were constructed using univariate analysis, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), and logistic regression. Model performance was assessed by cross-validation, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration, decision curve analysis, and clinical impact curve. Results Metastatic lymph nodes showed significantly lower central-to-peripheral ratios of density and velocity parameters but higher relative temporal changes in density SD and velocity SD compared with benign nodes (all P < .05). The static time-point model retained 2 SRUS variables (Mean.Density_C_P_T2, Max.Density_C_P_T3), yielding a full-sample AUC of 0.8607. The temporal change model included 2 dynamic parameters (Velocity SD change from T1 to T2, Mean density change from T2 to T3) and achieved a higher AUC of 0.8715, with better accuracy, specificity, and model fit. Both models showed favorable calibration and clinical net benefit. Conclusion Quantitative SRUS parameters effectively reflect pathological angiogenesis in metastatic lymph nodes. The temporal change model provides superior diagnostic performance over the static time-point model and may serve as a reliable noninvasive tool for distinguishing benign from metastatic lymph nodes.

title: Individualised total knee arthroplasty results in low reintervention rates for stiffness and instability in 1000 consecutive knees, regardless of intraoperative bone recuts or polyethylene thickness.
abstract: Purpose Individualised total knee arthroplasty (TKA) aims to restore the pre-arthritic anatomy, but concerns persist regarding ligament imbalance, as only two polyethylene insert thicknesses are available. This study aimed to evaluate revision and reintervention rates, especially for stiffness and instability, after individualised TKA, and whether intraoperative adjustments influenced these outcomes. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 1000 consecutive primary TKAs implanted using a CT-based individualised system with a 1-year minimum follow-up. The primary endpoint was any revision TKA. Secondary analyses evaluated reintervention for stiffness or instability and the association between reinterventions and (1) bone recuts and (2) polyethylene thickness. Survival was estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method. Results At a mean follow-up of 4.2 ± 1.8 years, 12 revision TKA (1.2%) and 29 reinterventions (2.9%) were recorded. All procedures were completed as planned with only two polyethylene insert thicknesses. Revision-free survival was 99.4% (95% confidence interval [CI] 98.7-99.7) at 1 year and 98.7% (95% CI 97.7-99.3) at 5 years. Reoperation-free survival was 98.1% (95% CI 97.0-98.8) and 97.0% (95% CI 95.7-97.9) at 1 and 5 years, respectively. Stiffness-related procedures occurred in nine cases (0.9%), and instability-related revision was observed in one case (0.1%). Bone recuts were performed in 42.8% of knees. No significant association was found between revision risk and bone recuts or polyethylene thickness. Conclusion In this large consecutive cohort, individualised TKA was associated with low rates of revision and of reintervention for stiffness and instability. Intraoperative adjustments (bone recuts, polyethylene thickness changes) were not associated with a higher revision rate. Level of evidence Level III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Gracilis tendon harvest for ACL reconstruction impairs gracilis muscle volume recovery and may adversely affect adjacent thigh musculature. MRI-based outcomes from a subgroup of patients enroled in the DOSTAR randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Purpose Segmentation of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows accurate calculation of muscle volumes. The Dual Or Single Tendon Anterior cruciate ligament Reconstruction (DOSTAR) study is a prospective randomized controlled trial investigating a semitendinosus (ST) graft with adjustable button tibial fixation versus a dual tendon semitendinosus and gracilis (STG) graft with screw tibial fixation in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). The purpose of the present study is to investigate differences in thigh muscle volume at 6 and 12 months between these treatment groups. Methods Patients were randomized and underwent ACLR using either a ST or STG graft construct. MRI of bilateral thighs was completed at 6 and 12 months post-operatively. Muscle volumes were measured in both thighs at both time points in both groups. Results A total of 38 patients underwent MRI scanning at 6 and 12 months. There was a significant difference in the interval volume change of gracilis in the STG group compared to the ST group (-1.6 cm 3 ± 4.6 vs. +2.8 cm 3 ± 6.8, p = 0.026). Interval gracilis hypertrophy occurred in 35% (7/20) of cases in the STG group and 67% of cases (12/18) in the ST group (p = 0.103). Adductor longus (AddL) also demonstrated a significant difference in interval volume change between the STG and ST group (-2.4 cm 3 ± 12.0 vs. +11.1 cm 3 ± 21.2, p = 0.020). AddL hypertrophy occurred in 30% of cases (6/20) in the STG group and 72% (13/18) in the ST group (p = 0.022). All other muscles had no significant differences noted in muscle recovery between groups. Linear regression analysis demonstrated a significant positive relationship between interval changes in gracilis and AddL volumes (p < 0.001). Conclusions The present study provides MRI evidence that gracilis tendon harvest was associated with persistent impairment of gracilis muscle recovery and may also adversely affect AddL. This adds to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of ST with adjustable button graft constructs for hamstring ACLR. Level of evidence Level II, subgroup analysis of prospective, double-blinded, randomized controlled trial.

title: Reliability-weighted patch learning for synthetic CT reconstruction in head and neck adaptive radiotherapy: A proof-of-concept study.
abstract: Background Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is essential for adaptive radiotherapy (ART) but is limited by poor image quality. Existing deep learning methods for synthetic CT (sCT) generation face a critical trade-off: diffusion models offer high fidelity but are impractically slow, while fast-inference networks often lack structural accuracy and optimization stability. Purpose To develop HQ-PatchNet, a reliability-driven deep learning framework designed to improve CBCT-to-sCT image quality while maintaining rapid inference speed for online ART workflows. Methods HQ-PatchNet utilizes a vision transformer (ViT)-integrated CycleGAN architecture. It introduces a reliability-driven, SSIM-based selective patch weighting mechanism controlled by a temperature decay schedule. This dynamically suppresses artifact-dominated regions and focuses optimization on anatomically reliable structures. The model was evaluated on 304 paired head-and-neck (HN) scans against conventional networks and recent diffusion models using quantitative metrics (MAE, SSIM, NCC, PSNR), computational speed, and clinical dosimetric accuracy (3D gamma index, 2%/2 mm). Results HQ-PatchNet improved image quality, reducing Mean Absolute Error (MAE) from 44.81 ± 11.24 HU to 11.85 ± 4.31 HU and achieving an SSIM of 0.960 ± 0.055, comparable to state-of-the-art diffusion models. Inference required only 6.42 ± 1.71 s per volume, compared to > 15 min for diffusion approaches. The model reduced severe metal and truncation artifacts, and representative qualitative assessment suggested visually consistent sCT generation under interfractional anatomical variation. Dosimetric assessment of complex HN IMRT plans yielded a high average gamma passing rate of 99.32 ± 0.56%. Conclusions HQ-PatchNet provides a computationally efficient and clinically promising approach for daily CBCT-guided online ART by improving CBCT-to-sCT image quality while maintaining rapid inference speed. Further contour-based, multi-institutional, and multi-site validation remains necessary to confirm its broader clinical utility.

title: Learning global and local representations for generalized category discovery in neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved notable success in closed-set classification of neurodegenerative diseases, but its performance degrades significantly in more realistic open-set settings, such as discovering rare or novel disease subtypes from unlabeled data that are not seen during training. This study introduces, to our knowledge, the first framework for generalized category discovery (GCD) in neurodegenerative diseases using MRI. It aims to leverage labeled data from known categories to automatically identify novel categories within unlabeled datasets. We propose a GCD framework integrating semi-supervised contrastive learning with global-local representation learning to jointly optimize feature learning. Globally, we enforce consistency between weakly augmented views of the same instance by aligning their similarity relationships with other embeddings in a support queue. Locally, we treat neighborhood embeddings from the support queue as positive pairs for cross-instance contrastive learning, enhancing fine-grained discrimination. This dual strategy results in a unified learning objective that is applicable to both labeled and unlabeled data, effectively narrowing the representation gap among semantically similar instances. We evaluate our method on a benchmark dataset comprising six neurodegenerative diseases, with over 1500 patient samples. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms representative state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, our method achieves 66.02% Accuracy and 60.59% Normalized Mutual Information on all categories, and 54.53% Accuracy and 16.67% Normalized Mutual Information on novel categories, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. Our framework underscores the model's robustness and its practical value in discovering new neurodegenerative disease conditions, highlighting its potential for advancing open-set diagnostic AI.

title: Impact of correlated PBPK parameters on intra-patient global sensitivity analysis in molecular radiotherapy.
abstract: Background Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models integrated into digital twins provide a robust framework for optimizing individualized molecular radiotherapy (MRT). Nevertheless, uncertainties in PBPK-model-derived dosimetry can compromise the reliability of dosimetry-guided treatment planning and individualized therapy decisions. Purpose This study employs intra-patient global sensitivity analysis (GSA) to assess the influence of uncertainty and correlations among PBPK model parameters on estimated kidney and tumor absorbed doses (ADs) in prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted theragnostics. Methods Data from 10 patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer who underwent pre-therapeutic [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-I&T PET/CT and a cycle of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-I&T therapy, followed by post-therapeutic SPECT/CT scans at Days 1 and 4 post-injection, were analyzed. A previously established whole-body PBPK model for PSMA-targeted radionuclide therapy was used as the baseline model. Fifteen model parameters, their standard errors, and inter-parameter correlations were estimated by fitting to measured time-activity data and subsequently evaluated using intra-patient GSA based on the Kucherenko method implemented in UQLab. In one approach, correlations were ignored to identify the direct influences of uncertainty in input parameters on ADs. In a second approach, correlations were included to reflect realistic parameter distributions and to capture indirect effects arising from parameter interdependencies. Pharmacokinetics were simulated to estimate therapeutic kidney and tumor ADs as well as main- and total-effect indices ( Si,SiT) . Sensitivity indices, ADs, and their associated uncertainty metrics were compared between scenarios with and without parameter correlations. Results Including parameter correlations in the GSA yielded kidney ADs of 4.2 Gy [3.0-7.2 Gy] (median [min-max]) with standard deviations (SDs) of 0.5 Gy [0.4-0.9 Gy] and tumor ADs of 10.1 Gy [2.0-26.8 Gy] with SDs of 1.7 Gy [0.6-3.4 Gy]. Neglecting correlations resulted in significantly higher uncertainties in ADs, by a factor of 1.2 [1.0-1.8] for both kidneys and tumors. Kidney ADs were most sensitive to kidney receptor density ( Si=0.3[0.1-0.6], SiT=0.7[0.6-0.8] ) and to the filtered fraction of renal blood flow (Si=0.2[0.1-0.3], SiT=0.3[0.1-0.4]) . Tumor ADs were most affected by tumor receptor density ( Si=0.7[0.1-1.0], SiT=0.8[0.3-1.0] ). The involvement of parameter correlations did not alter the identification of the parameters most influential on AD estimates and further reduced computational runtime. Conclusions Incorporating parameter correlations into intra-patient GSA reduced the estimated uncertainty associated with ADs, underscoring the importance of preserving parameter dependencies when propagating uncertainty in PBPK-based individualized MRT. The identification of key PBPK parameters governing kidney and tumor ADs remained stable when including correlation, confirming the robustness of the underlying model structure.

title: An anatomy-aware spatio-temporal generative extrapolation network for distal ascending aorta restoration in standard echocardiographic views.
abstract: Background In two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), the standard parasternal long-axis (PLAX) view enables reliable evaluation of the aortic valve and aortic root. Owing to the limited field of view of the ultrasound probe and rib-window occlusion, the distal ascending aorta (AA) is frequently truncated, compromising the diagnosis of aortic aneurysm and dilation. Purpose We aim to address the incomplete visualization of the distal AA in standard PLAX views. By aggregating fragmented anatomical features intermittently visible in adjacent frames, we enhance the clarity of vessel wall edges and generate the distal AA structure, thereby completing the missing AA imagery in standard PLAX views. Materials and methods We retrospectively collected 1160 TTE videos from Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital (August 2022 - December 2024), all showing complete AA anatomy. After de-identification, 1059 cases were randomly split into training/validation/test sets (6:2:2), and 101 cases were reserved for observer agreement experiments. An additional 152 videos from three different device models (EPIQ CVX, GE Voluson E10, Resona A20T) formed an external validation set. Two training data types were constructed: (i) dual-view synchronous data - a standard PLAX sequence and an AO-PLAX sequence acquired after a cranial probe shift, phase-matched at end diastole (ED); and (ii) locally masked data - the distal AA region was masked, forcing the model to infer missing anatomy from left-side context. Input sequences of five frames (ED ± 2) were extracted. The proposed Spatio-Temporal Ascending-Aorta generative adversarial network (STAA-GAN) first aligns adjacent frames using an Edge Boosted Feature Alignment (EBFA) module with multi-stage modulated deformable convolutions. A channel-wise fusion strategy then aggregates temporally aligned features. The fused representation is fed into a Swin-UNet generator enhanced with a Strip based Cross window Prediction (SCP) module to capture long-range structural dependencies. Training employs a composite loss including pixel reconstruction, feature reconstruction, texture consistency, relativistic average least-squares GAN (RaLSGAN), temporal coherence, and structure-aware terms, with data-dependent weighting. Statistical analyzes included Bland-Altman, Passing-Bablok regression, paired t-tests with Cohen's d, Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, and two one-sided tests (TOST, Δ=0.2cm ). Results STAA-GAN achieved the best image-quality values among the compared methods, with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) = 22.51 dB, structural similarity index (SSIM) = 0.7574, multi-scale structural similarity index (MS-SSIM) = 0.8598, and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) = 0.1758. All 12 pairwise comparisons (SRN, IOH, and U-Transformer versus STAA-GAN, designated as the reference group) remained statistically significant after Bonferroni correction ( α1=0.00417 ), with absolute effect sizes ranging from 0.255 to 3.439. The per-frame inference time was 203 ms. In clinical consistency validation, the mean difference between measurements on generated and original images was ≤0.01 cm with 95% limits of agreement within ±0.13 cm; TOST with Δ=0.2 cm confirmed clinical equivalence for all comparisons ( p<0.001 ). The segmentation Dice coefficient on generated images averaged 0.913±0.045 across five cross-validation folds. External validation on three different ultrasound devices (Philips, GE, Mindray) maintained consistent equivalence (TOST p<0.001 , Cohen's d<0.2 ). These results demonstrate that STAA-GAN produces clinically interchangeable distal ascending aorta images with high fidelity and real-time feasibility. Conclusions STAA-GAN enables extrapolation of the missing distal ascending aorta in standard PLAX views, achieving improved image quality and clinically equivalent diameter measurements on both internal and external validation datasets. These findings support its potential for assisting distal ascending aorta assessment in routine echocardiography.

title: Free-breathing fast abdominal simultaneous T<sub>1</sub>, T<sub>2</sub>, PD and B<sub>1</sub> mapping via deep learning reconstruction.
abstract: Background Multi-parametric quantitative MRI (mqMRI) enables non-invasive tissue characterization and holds significant clinical value in abdominal imaging. Conventional methods are restricted by long acquisition times and motion artifacts induced by physiological processes and irregular breathing, leading to registration errors between sequential acquisitions. Purpose To develop and evaluate a framework for abdominal quantitative imaging under free-breathing conditions with reduced scan time and improved robustness to motion. Methods A novel framework integrating the longitudinal magnetization-controlled multiple overlapping-echo detachment (LMC-MOLED) sequence with synthetic data-driven deep learning reconstruction was proposed. To generate the synthetic dataset for training, a respiratory motion model combining global and local displacement vector fields was developed, ensuring temporal alignment with the inter-phase intervals of LMC-MOLED acquisitions. By applying interpolation to the original template, virtual imaging objects were generated to simulate respiratory-induced deformations while preserving anatomical textures, tissue boundaries, and inter-slice correlations. These objects were subsequently processed with MRI Bloch simulation to generate the final synthetic dataset, which was used to train a BGA-Multi-UNet architecture for motion correction and improved quantitative accuracy. Results The proposed framework enabled simultaneous mapping of T 1 , T 2 , proton density, and B 1 under free-breathing conditions. With a 5-slice interleaved acquisition, the average acquisition time was reduced to approximately one second per slice without the need for respiratory gating. Both numerical and in vivo experiments demonstrated high accuracy and repeatability, with image quality comparable to conventional breath-hold acquisitions while mitigating motion-induced artifacts. Conclusion This framework offers a rapid and reliable solution for multi-parametric abdominal imaging under free-breathing conditions. The combination of synthetic motion modeling with deep learning reconstruction enables accurate quantitative mapping with effective motion correction, offering potential clinical benefits for efficient and robust abdominal magnetic resonance imaging.

title: Rep2Rep-Shuffle: Shuffled Repetition-to-Repetition Learning for Noise-Adaptive Self-Supervised MRI Denoising.
abstract: Purpose MRI applications with low SNR, such as non-proton imaging and low-field imaging, often require multiple signal averages to achieve adequate image quality at the cost of longer scan times. This work proposes Rep2Rep-Shuffle, a self-supervised learning framework that improves MRI denoising performance in repeated-acquisition imaging with limited training datasets. Methods Rep2Rep-Shuffle extends our previously proposed repetition-to-repetition learning (Rep2Rep)-based self-supervised denoising approach with a new shuffled repetition pairing strategy. Instead of using a fixed split between training input and target repetitions, different repetition combinations are randomly generated during training epochs for each dataset, which increases the effective training space when training datasets are limited. In addition, the framework also extends from slice-wise 2D to 3D denoising by exploiting correlations across all spatial dimensions. The proposed method was tested in vivo using sodium MRI and further validated using synthetic noisy MRI datasets. Different training strategies for both 2D and 3D denoising were compared. Results In vivo sodium MRI results demonstrated improved denoising and better preservation of anatomical structures with 3D Rep2Rep-Shuffle compared with fixed pairing (Rep2Rep) and 2D denoising. Reader evaluation further confirmed that 3D Rep2Rep-Shuffle received higher scores for different assessment categories. In synthetic experiments, 3D Rep2Rep-Shuffle achieved the best performance among self-supervised methods and approached the performance of supervised learning. Conclusion Rep2Rep-Shuffle outperforms Rep2Rep for MRI denoising by increasing training diversity through shuffled repetition pairing and by leveraging volumetric spatial correlations. The method is particularly suited for low-SNR MRI applications that acquire multiple repetitions but have limited training datasets.

In synthetic experiments, 3D Rep2Rep-Shuffle achieved the best performance among self-supervised methods and approached the performance of supervised learning.

Conclusion

Rep2Rep-Shuffle outperforms Rep2Rep for MRI denoising by increasing training diversity through shuffled repetition pairing and by leveraging volumetric spatial correlations. The method is particularly suited for low-SNR MRI applications that acquire multiple repetitions but have limited training datasets.

title: Deep-Reorder: Refined Motion Correction for 3D Brain MRI via Iterative Data Regrouping.
abstract: Purpose Accurate and temporally high-resolution estimation of subject motion is paramount for effective motion-correction in MRI. This work proposes a novel approach for estimating subject motion within a 3D MRI scan with high temporal resolution. Methods Starting from an incoherent sampling scheme, images are reconstructed from temporally ordered k-space fractions via deep learning, enabling motion estimation via registration between each image. Assuming the bulk of the motion is removed using these initial estimates, the remaining misalignment between k-space fractions is expected to be minimally correlated in time. Based on this insight, an iterative strategy is proposed in which shots are arbitrarily regrouped into new k-space fractions, regardless of their original temporal ordering, for subsequent motion estimation and correction. This effectively increases the temporal resolution of the approach, enabling individual correction of all shots. Results When applied to 3D T1w TFE MRI of the brain, the proposed approach "Deep-Reorder" estimated a unique motion state for all shots, producing significantly better estimations of retrospective motion compared to estimation without iterative data regrouping. On prospectively motion-corrupted scans with intentional head movement by volunteers, the proposed approach consistently improved image quality, producing less noisy images with reduced motion artifacts. Conclusion In conclusion, the proposed approach, which is free of external tracking devices or navigators, effectively estimated 3D motion and corrected motion artifacts with increased temporal resolution.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Magnetic Resonance Elastography Versus Vibration-Controlled Transient Elastography for Liver Fibrosis Staging in Steatotic Liver Disease.
abstract: Gravitational magnetic resonance elastography (GT-MRE) enables comprehensive biomechanical liver characterization and may overcome limitations of conventional elastography techniques. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of two- and three-dimensional (2D and 3D) GT-MRE compared with 2D acoustic MRE (AC-MRE) and vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE) for liver fibrosis staging. In this prospective study, patients with suspected or known steatotic liver disease underwent GT-MRE (2D and 3D, gradient-echo sequences) and AC-MRE (2D, spin-echo echo-planar imaging) at 1.5 T, plus VCTE with a median interval to MRE of 37 days (IQR, 20-124 days; range, 0-372 days). Statistical analyses included generalized additive models, ordinal logistic regression, and decision tree-based classification. Diagnostic performance was assessed using cumulative receiver operating characteristic analysis and corresponding areas under the curve (AUCs). Ninety-one participants (median age, 55 years [IQR, 45-64]; 41 women) were included, of whom 35 (38%) had histopathological correlation. In the biopsy-confirmed subgroup, 3D GT-MRE-derived viscoelastic parameters showed promising exploratory performance for early fibrosis classification. Wave attenuation achieved AUCs of 0.91 for F0 versus ≥ F1 and 0.99 for ≤ F1 versus ≥ F2, while phase angle yielded an AUC of 0.88 for F0 versus ≥ F1, with numerically higher AUCs than conventional stiffness-based metrics. For advanced fibrosis thresholds, all modalities performed well (AUC ≥ 0.84). Obuchowski measures for 3D-derived parameters were 0.95-0.96. Internally cross-validated multiparametric modeling achieved an accuracy of up to 92%. VCTE measurements plateaued beyond F3, whereas AC- and GT-MRE metrics continued to increase with fibrosis severity. 3D GT-MRE-derived viscoelastic parameters showed promising performance for liver fibrosis classification and provided biomechanical information complementary to conventional stiffness measurements. Given the limited biopsy-confirmed sample and marked class imbalance at F0, these findings require validation in larger independent cohorts before clinical implementation.

title: The Associations Between Olfactory Bulb Morphology, Volume Change, and Olfactory Recovery.
abstract: Objective To investigate whether olfactory bulb (OB) morphology is associated with olfactory recovery following olfactory training (OT) in individuals with COVID-19-related smell loss. Study design Prospective observational study. Setting University hospital and research center. Methods Twenty women with COVID-19-associated olfactory dysfunction and 19 healthy controls underwent OT for 3 months. OB shape (oval vs non-oval) was classified using high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and bilateral OB volumes were manually segmented before and after OT. Olfactory performance was assessed with the Sniffin' Sticks test. Statistical analyses included independent t tests, multimodal analysis of covariance, correlation analyses, and generalized estimating equations. Results At baseline, OB volume correlated significantly with olfactory performance. Changes in left OB volume were positively correlated with changes in odor threshold. Following OT, patients with non-oval OB shapes showed greater improvement in Threshold + Discrimination + Identification (TDI) scores and enlargement of left OB volume compared to those with oval-shaped OB. However, OB morphology did not significantly change over time in both patients and controls. Conclusion OB shape may provide a novel perspective for predicting prognosis after OT. Further studies with larger cohorts and extended training durations are warranted to validate these preliminary observations.

title: Thoracic Endometriosis Mimicking a Lung Mass: Management With Single-Stage Biopsy and Microwave Ablation.
abstract: Thoracic endometriosis syndrome is a rare extrapelvic manifestation involving the pleura, diaphragm or lung parenchyma. Presentation as a solitary pulmonary nodule mimicking malignancy is uncommon. We report a 31-year-old asymptomatic woman with an enlarging right lower lobe nodule, measuring 1.8-2.1 cm over 3 months. Following shared decision-making, single-stage image-guided biopsy and microwave ablation (MWA) were performed. Histopathology confirmed pulmonary endometriosis. No clinically significant postoperative complications occurred, and the patient was discharged on postoperative Day 1. Follow-up CT at 6 and 12 months demonstrated no obvious local recurrence without additional treatment. This case describes a potential minimally invasive approach for selected pulmonary lesions, although the safety, efficacy and long-term outcomes of MWA for pulmonary endometriosis remain uncertain.

title: Tunable <sup>18</sup>F-Labeling of Erlotinib-Based Small Molecule Nanodrugs for Rapid PET Imaging and Targeted Therapy.
abstract: Small molecule nanodrugs (SMNs) offer unique advantages for cancer therapy, yet accurately tracking their in vivo fate without perturbing their native assembly remains challenging. Here, we report a spacer engineering strategy that enables efficient 1 8 F-labeling while preserving SMNs self-assembly. Erlotinib-based amphiphilic derivatives containing oligoethylene glycol (OEG) spacers of tunable length were designed to simultaneously regulate steric hindrance for aliphatic S N 2 radiofluorination and the amphiphilic balance required for nanoparticle formation. Spacer elongation reduced steric hindrance at the labeling site and thereby improved radiochemical yields, while also enabling precise control over nanoparticle size. The optimized radiolabeled formulation, [ 18 F]E3F NPs , exhibited prolonged blood circulation and rapid tumor accumulation, enabling high-contrast PET imaging of PANC-1 xenografts as early as 15 min after injection. In addition, the corresponding nonradioactive formulation, E3F NPs , showed significantly improved antitumor efficacy compared with nonassembled E3F through reduced EGFR phosphorylation and increased tumor cell apoptosis. This work provides an initial evaluation that spacer engineering can coordinate radiolabeling and self-assembly while enabling PET tracking of SMNs, supporting the development of image-guided cancer theranostics.
