title: In-vivo MRI of noradrenergic and dopaminergic nuclei predicts future cognition and Alzheimers disease progression
abstract: Noradrenergic and dopaminergic nuclei modulate cognition, and post-mortem data indicate they are affected early in the neurodegenerative cascade of Alzheimers disease. We derived in-vivo locus coeruleus (LC) and substantia nigra-ventral tegmental area (SN-VTA) MRI integrity measures from 739 ADNI participants, examined MRI-histology correspondence in individuals with both in-vivo imaging and post-mortem data, and tested whether these measures reflect early MRI-indexed degeneration predicting later cognitive decline. LC and SN-VTA contrast predicted cognitive and behavioral function 10 years later, despite only weak associations with current function. LC- and SN-VTA-associated brain-wide atrophy patterns aligned with PET-derived norepinephrine-transporter and dopamine-receptor maps, respectively. A one-standard-deviation decrease in baseline LC contrast was associated with 84% higher five-year odds of MCI-to-AD progression, and predictive effects of the catecholaminergic nuclei were mediated by their corresponding atrophy patterns. The SN-VTA pattern was associated with less amyloid PET-related memory decline. Together, these findings establish LC and SN-VTA MRI contrast as markers of early neurodegeneration that forecast cognitive decline years before clinical onset.

title: Agreement of abdominal palpation with point-of-care ultrasound for hepatosplenic organomegaly: a cross-sectional, population-based study in schistosomiasis-endemic settings of rural Uganda
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Ultrasound is commonly used to assess hepatosplenic morbidity in schistosomiasis, but access may be limited in resource-constrained settings. Abdominal palpation is simple and inexpensive, yet its clinical value and diagnostic performance for detecting ultrasound-defined organ enlargement remains uncertain. We evaluated standardised abdominal palpation against point-of-care ultrasound in a schistosomiasis-endemic setting in rural Uganda. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional study in January-February 2024 of 3177 participants aged 5-92 years from Pakwach, Buliisa and Mayuge districts in the SchistoTrack cohort. Trained nurses who also had midwifery skills performed standardised liver and spleen palpation, assessing palpability, extension, consistency and tenderness. Palpation agreement was assessed against point-of-care B-mode ultrasound performed by sonographers with organ dimensions classified using height-standardised internal reference values. We estimated sensitivity, specificity, predictive values and Cohen’s κ for palpation against ultrasound-defined liver and spleen enlargement and assessed associations between liver consistency and tenderness, and schistosomal periportal fibrosis examined from ultrasound. Results Spleen palpation had high specificity (98.4%), with sensitivity ranging from 10.9% for moderate splenomegaly to 48.6% for severe splenomegaly. There was strong agreement with ultrasound for severe splenomegaly (κ=0.57) though weak agreement for moderate splenomegaly (κ=0.14). Liver palpation had high specificity (97.7%) but very low sensitivity (3.4-7.3%) and minimal agreement with any hepatomegaly found from ultrasound (κ=0.02-0.04). Among participants with a palpable liver, schistosomal periportal fibrosis was more frequent in those with firm/hard than soft liver consistency (53.3%, n=24/45 vs 8.6%, n=3/35; χ²=17.64, p<0.001); while tenderness was not associated with schistosomal periportal fibrosis. Nurses additionally identified clinically relevant findings, including umbilical collaterals, abdominal swelling, and abdominal or hypochondrial pain and tenderness. Conclusions Standardised abdominal palpation cannot replace ultrasound for comprehensive detection or exclusion of hepatosplenomegaly. Nevertheless, severe ultrasound-defined splenomegaly was more readily detected by palpation, while liver consistency and other clinical findings provided information beyond organomegaly. In schistosomiasis-endemic settings with limited access to ultrasound, further research is needed to assess building capacity for abdominal palpation and how it can be combined with clinical information to increase clinical suspicion while possibly informing low-cost strategies for triage and referral.

title: Ophthalmic AI With Just Ten Examples: Comparing Multimodal Large Language Models, Vision Foundation Models, and Vision-Language Models
abstract: Purpose: To compare multimodal large language models (MLLMs), vision foundation models (VFMs), and contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) for ophthalmic image interpretation with no labeled examples (zero-shot) or as few as 10 labeled examples per class (10-shot). Design: Retrospective benchmarking study. Subjects: 4 public datasets (UCSD, IDRiD, REFUGE, ASOCT-MSDC) and 3 private datasets (OHTS, BPEI-DLS, WashU-OCT) of anterior- and posterior-segment ophthalmic imaging. Methods: Nine AI models were evaluated across 3 architectural families: MLLMs (Qwen3.8-27B, GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemma-4-31B-it), VFMs (DINOv3, RETFound, VisionFM), and VLMs (CLIP, EyeCLIP, SigLIP2). Models were assessed on disease classification, disease risk and severity grading, anatomical assessment, and lesion localization in fundus and OCT imaging. MLLMs were also compared with a 3D VFM (OCTCube-M) for whole-volume OCT classification. MLLMs were evaluated zero-shot and 10-shot, without additional training. Vision models (VFMs and VLMs) were adapted by linear probing and fine-tuning on the same 10-shot set and on the full training dataset (FD). Main Outcome Measures: Disease classification performance (macro-averaged F1, AUROC, quadratic weighted kappa [QWK]), anatomical localization accuracy, and cross-dataset generalization. Results: For retinal OCT disease classification, 10-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.94, versus 0.59 (10-shot) and 0.96 (FD) for vision models. For diabetic retinopathy and macular edema grading, 10-shot MLLMs achieved QWKs of 0.69 and 0.73, versus 0.48 and 0.57 (10-shot) and 0.72 and 0.79 (FD) for vision models. For lesion localization, 10-shot MLLMs achieved an F1 of 0.75, versus 0.70 (10-shot) and 0.86 (FD) for vision models. For vertical cup-to-disc ratio estimation (OHTS), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a mean absolute error of 0.14, versus 0.21 (10-shot) for vision models. For whole-volume OCT classification (WashU-OCT), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.71, versus 0.50 (10-shot) and 0.82 (FD) for vision models. Conclusions: Open-weight MLLMs given 10 labeled examples per class outperformed VFMs and VLMs trained on the same examples in most tasks and approached the performance of fully trained VFMs and VLMs in selected disease classification and grading tasks. MLLMs also demonstrated promising zero-shot performance on non-public clinical datasets without task-specific training. By reducing the need for large labeled datasets and task-specific model adaptation, MLLMs could broaden who can develop and validate ophthalmic AI.

title: Lesion-Derived Estimated Functional and Structural Connectomes Predict Post-Stroke Recovery Outcomes
abstract: Accurate prognosis after stroke remains challenging, limiting the ability to predict individual recovery. While advanced connectome MRI can provide further prognostically-useful information regarding affected brain networks, its impractical nature has given rise instead to lesion-based estimates of network disruptions. Here, we present a novel pipeline that leverages our recently developed connectome analysis tools to estimate structural disconnection (eSDC) and functional connectivity (eFC) directly from N=96 patient lesion masks for use in predicting motor, language, attention and memory outcomes at multiple timepoints after stroke. Our approach jointly leverages our Network Modification (NeMo) Tool, a database of white matter tractography results that estimates structural disconnectivity (eSDC), and the Krakencoder, a joint autoencoder that estimates functional connectomes (eFC) from the NeMo Tool's output. Models based on eSDC and eFC predicted almost all outcomes, particularly motor outcomes, significantly better than models that used patients' fMRI-based observed FC (oFC) and models based on only lesion information and covariates. Estimated connectome measures also i) retained meaningful inter-individual variability when compared to observed functional connectomes, ii) reflected population-level, stroke-related changes in functional connectomes, and iii) resulted in outcome prediction models with feature importances that aligned with expected networks of relevance to the given outcome. Feature importance analyses also identified distinct predictive signatures across both modality and outcome domain, indicating that eSDC and eFC capture non-redundant, biologically meaningful information about post-stroke network disruption. Together, these findings establish our lesion-based estimates of post-stroke structural and functional connectomes as a practical, information-rich alternative to advanced imaging in patients. This approach allows for probing an individual's affected neural circuitry underlying stroke impairment and recovery, paving the way toward more efficient, accessible, and personalized approaches to post-stroke prognosis and intervention.

title: How Well Does Structural MRI Classify Autism? A Leakage-Free, Site-Aware and Externally Validated Machine-Learning Evaluation in Two ABIDE Cohorts
abstract: Background: Many studies report high accuracy for classifying autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from structural MRI, but small samples, single train-test splits, site effects and information leakage can inflate performance. We evaluated how well brain morphometry distinguishes autistic from typically developing (TD) individuals under rigorous, leakage-free validation. Methods: FreeSurfer-derived features (n = 280: regional thickness, area and volume; subcortical volumes; Yeo-network composites; asymmetry indices; global measures) from ABIDE II (804 participants; 341 ASD; 12 sites) were used to train logistic regression, linear support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost and multilayer perceptron classifiers. Confound regression (age, age2, sex, brain volume), site-wise centring and standardisation were learned within training folds only. Performance was assessed with nested 10-fold cross-validation, leave-one-site-out validation and external validation in ABIDE I (917 participants; 20 sites), and compared with full-pipeline permutation tests and a confound-only baseline. Results: Cross-validated discrimination was modest: the best model (regularised logistic regression on all features) reached an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.60 [0.56, 0.64], significantly above chance (permutation p = .002) but far from clinically useful and below a confound-only baseline using age, sex, brain volume and site (AUC 0.63); non-linear models did not perform better (AUC 0.45-0.60 across models and feature sets). Pooled leave-one-site-out AUCs were 0.54-0.61, with large between-site variation, and AUCs in the external ABIDE I cohort were 0.52-0.58. Age-stratified models did not exceed AUC 0.60. Across 300 random 80/20 splits in young adults, test-set AUCs ranged from 0.21 to 0.90, showing that single-split estimates such as 0.74 can arise by chance. Conclusions: Under leakage-free, site-aware and externally validated evaluation, structural MRI morphometry classifies autism only slightly better than chance. Reports of high accuracy should be interpreted with caution, and the heterogeneity of autism argues for stratification and normative approaches rather than binary diagnostic classifiers.

title: Strategies of mechanical adaptations of circulating tumor cells and properties of their cellular microenvironment have predictive and prognostic biomarker value
abstract: Mechanically demanding conditions in the blood circulation damage and kill majority of tumor-shed circulating tumor cells (CTCs). Mechanical fitness: a set of mechanical properties detected with atomic force spectroscopy based force spectrometry supports survival of CTCs. We propose that live CTCs isolated from peripheral blood of prostate cancer patients represent distinct strategies of fitness promoting mechanical adaptations to the fluid shear stress. Some of the cells mimicked properties of erythrocytes (high stiffness) or leukocytes (high deformability). The clustering strategy characterized by exceptionally high adhesion is ingenious to CTCs and not found in blood cells. The abundance of CTCs with elevated adhesion has a predictive value for prostate cancer patients starting first round of androgen deprivation therapy. Moreover, a high adhesion score based on individual cells or average patient-specific adhesion is instrumental to stratify recurrent patients that underwent diagnostic imaging by PSMA-PET/CT and clarify inconclusive PSMA scan results. Including contribution of erythrocyte-like strategy broadened the predictive power of CTC mechanophenotyping. Improved biomarking opportunities to predict early castration resistances were noted when the composition of CTC microenvironment was included alongside the mechanical properties. We demonstrated previously that the CTC microenvironment is formed by large cells co-purifying by microfiltration of the blood of cancer patients. Analysis of the association of particular components of CTC microenvironment with the clustering strategy led to pointing at highly adhesive CTC-EMT. However, in the advanced patients adhesiveness of CTC-EMT was surpassed by tumor hybrid cells (THCs), a distinctive kind of invasive species formed by incomplete phagocytosis of CTCs by macrophages. THCs changed their mechanical phenotype and strategy preference with disease progression pointing at the dynamic nature of adaptations of tumor-shed cells to circulation conditions.

title: 2D U-NET Deep Learning Architecture for Atherosclerotic Lesion Segmentation and Quantification
abstract: Mice are commonly used for experimental atherosclerosis research, and a common procedure involves morphometric analysis of atherosclerotic lesions on Oil Red O-stained cross-sections of the aortic root. However, manual measurement of atherosclerotic lesion sizes on numerous histological sections is tedious and time-consuming. Here, we developed a deep learning model based on convolutional neural network to quantify atherosclerotic lesions in cross-sectioned aortic roots of mice. Microscopy images were taken from cross-sectioned aortic roots of genetically diverse F2 mice derived from BALB/cJ and LP/J Apoe knockout mice and fed 12 weeks of a Western diet. Aortic cross-sections were stained with Oil Red O and hematoxylin and images captured. Atherosclerotic lesions were manually segmented in 2553 images using Zeiss AxioVision. These images were split into 1,533 for training the U-NET model, 510 for validation, and 510 images for testing. The developed model was evaluated for its performance to measure atherosclerotic lesions by comparing with manual measurement in test images. The model achieved a high degree of accuracy, with an F1 score of 0.82, a Jaccard score of 0.72, a Recall of 0.80, a precision of 0.87, and a correlation coefficient value of 0.98. While manual lesion measurement took approximately 5 minutes per image, the model performed the task in ~3.35 seconds, reducing measurement time by 98.9%. The developed 2D U-NET model provides a new platform for rapid and accurate quantification of atherosclerotic lesion sizes on Oil Red O-stained sections.

title: MaxCAT-Net: Hybrid Transformer-Based Skin Lesion Classification and Lightweight Segmentation with Calibration and Cross-Dataset Validation
abstract: Class imbalance, poor confidence calibration, and limited generalization under varying imaging conditions are major challenges in automated dermoscopic skin lesion analysis. We propose a hybrid classifier, MaxCAT-Net (MaxViT + CBAM + Attention Transformer), consisting of a pretrained MaxViT-Tiny backbone combined with CBAM and a lightweight two-layer Transformer encoder. We also evaluate four encoder-decoder networks for lesion segmentation as a separate task using ISIC 2018 Task 1. After removing exact and near-duplicate images, the remaining 10,012 images were divided into lesion-wise training, validation, and test sets using a 72/14/14 split, ensuring that images from the same lesion did not appear across multiple subsets. On the test set (n = 1,405), MaxCAT-Net outperformed the ResNet152-CBAM, MobileNetV3-CBAM, GhostNet-hybrid, and standalone MaxViT-Tiny-CBAM baselines, achieving an accuracy of 0.869 (95% CI: 0.847-0.890), balanced accuracy of 0.742, macro-F1 of 0.751, and macro-AUC of 0.944. However, ablation-related macro-F1 improvements (0.017-0.022) were not statistically conclusive. Temperature scaling reduced the expected calibration error (ECE) from 0.099 to 0.038. On the PAD-UFES-20 dataset, accuracy decreased to 0.341 and melanoma recall to 0.096, while melanoma recall on HAM10000 was only 0.587. For segmentation, a Swin-T-encoder U-Net achieved a Dice score of 0.903 on 520 test images, whereas a FasterNet-T0 U-Net, with approximately one-tenth the number of parameters, achieved a Dice score of 0.901 (Holm-adjusted p < 0.002). A standard U-Net achieved a significantly lower Dice score of 0.888. All results are based on a single random seed and should therefore be interpreted as preliminary trends rather than definitive evidence of improvement.
authorString: Prince SA, Shorna IF.

title: Deep learning grading of Schistosoma japonicum-associated liver ﬁbrosis from ultrasound images: a weighted soft-voting ensemble of convolutional and transformer networks
abstract: Background: Schistosomiasis morbidity still persists in China despite extensive progress towards elimination of new and active infections. Diagnosis of liver fibrosis related to Schistosoma japonicum remains challenging due to the subjective nature of ultrasound grading and the shortage of experienced sonographers in endemic counties. Methods: We developed a deep learning model that grades schistosomal liver fibrosis from a single B-mode ultrasound image without manual delineation of a region of interest. We used 2,921 images from 2,921 adults (aged 18-88 years, median age 54 years; 46.4% female) from a schistosomiasis hospital in Jiangxi Province, China, between 2019 and 2023. Of these, 12.9%, 34.6%, 32.4% and 20.2% had grade 0, 1, 2 and 3 fibrosis, respectively. Fibrosis grades were based on the clinical ultrasound record and re-evaluation by an experienced radiologist according to the Chinese Handbook of Schistosomiasis Control; discordant cases were reviewed by a second radiologist and resolved by consensus. Predictions from four neural networks with different architectures (ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet-121 and Swin-T) were combined by weighted soft voting, with weights derived from validation performance. Results: For the four-grade task this model achieved a macro-F1 of 0.8527 (95% CI 0.8184-0.8856), an accuracy of 0.8500 (0.8136-0.8818) and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.9187 (0.8983-0.9373) on a fixed test set of 440 images. For detecting significant fibrosis (grade 2 or 3; test-set prevalence 0.530), sensitivity was 0.9700, specificity was 0.9179, positive predictive value was 0.9300, negative predictive value was 0.9645, and AUROC was 0.9817. The ensemble achieved a higher macro-F1 than each individual backbone. Every ensemble misclassification was to an adjacent grade; no image with severe fibrosis was classified as no or mild fibrosis, or vice versa, whereas each individual backbone made 1-4 errors spanning two or more grades. Conclusions: The model may provide an automated aid for Schistosoma japonicum-associated fibrosis grading and could potentially support screening and follow-up in endemic areas after external validation.

title: Screening for rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease using lung ultrasound: a systematic review and quality appraisal of recent studies
abstract: Interstitial lung diseases (ILD) associated with systemic autoimmune disease can have a strong negative impact on patient outcomes. The diagnostic gold standard is high-resolution computer tomography (HRCT). Numerous studies have proven lung ultrasound's (LUS) utility in ILD, as well as other lung pathologies. Recently, there has been more focus on ILD in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a previously overlooked complication, and screening methods. The purpose of this systematic review was to summarize the recent knowledge regarding LUS compared to HRCT in screening ILD in RA patients. We reviewed relevant literature from the last 10 years and selected 10 articles. Results show that LUS is effective compared to HRCT as a screening tool. Several diagnostic and severity scores have been elaborated and tested. Further focus should be on LUS in long-term follow-up and standardization of protocols.

title: ACCURACY OF COMPRESSED SENSING ACCELERATED 3D-FLAIR IN THE DIAGNOSTIC WORK-UP OF MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS AT 1.5 T
abstract: BACKGROUND: 3D-FLAIR is central to MR-based diagnosis and monitoring of MS, but long acquisition times remain a limitation. OBJECTIVES: This single-center prospective non-inferiority study evaluated whether compressed sensing (CS) - accelerated 3D-FLAIR at 1.5T provides lesion detection comparable to optimized Generalized Autocalibrating Partially Parallel Acquisition (GRAPPA) - accelerated 3D-FLAIR. Optimized CS- and GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-FLAIR sequences were incorporated into MRI examinations in patients with known or suspected MS. The primary endpoint was manual lesion count by two blinded readers using a 10% non-inferiority margin. Secondary endpoints included image quality, SNR, CNR, and automated lesion count and volumetry. RESULTS: Sixty-eight patients were included (mean age, 40.1+/-13.3 years; 61.8% women). CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR reduced acquisition time by 31.8% compared with GRAPPA (4:00 vs 5:52 minutes). Non-inferiority for manual lesion count was demonstrated for both readers (reader A, p < .0001; reader B, p = .005). Interrater agreement was excellent for CS (ICC = 0.921; 95% CI, 0.837-0.957) and very good for GRAPPA (ICC = 0.851; 95% CI, 0.769-0.906). Subjective image quality was high for both techniques. GRAPPA showed higher objective signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise-ratio (CNR), whereas automated lesion counts and volumes were higher for CS. CONCLUSION: CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR provided non-inferior lesion detection with substantial scan-time reduction.

title: PROSPECTIVE COMPARISON OF OPTIMIZED COMPRESSED SENSING AND GRAPPA-ACCELERATED 3D-TOF-MRA FOR EVALUATION OF UNTREATED INTRACRANIAL ANEURYSMS AT 1.5 T: A NON-INFERIORITY STUDY
abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES 3D-TOF-MRA is a standard non-invasive method for detecting and monitoring intracranial aneurysms, but long scan times remain a limitation. Compressed sensing (CS) acceleration for intracranial aneurysm evaluation has mainly been studied at 3T. This prospective single-center non-inferiority study compared CS-accelerated 3D-TOF at 1.5T with GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-TOF-MRA for evaluating untreated intracranial aneurysms. MATERIALS AND METHODS Sample size was determined via a preliminary retrospective study. 25 patients with 32 untreated aneurysms underwent both CS- (factor 7, 3:04 min) and GRAPPA-accelerated (factor 2, 5:00 min) 3D-TOF, yielding a 38.7% scan-time reduction. Two blinded neuroradiologists assessed overall image quality (primary endpoint) and artifacts, subjective CNR, aneurysm delineation and diameters (secondary endpoints). Non-inferiority was tested via one-sided t-test (prespecified 10% margin); interrater agreement used ICC. RESULTS CS demonstrated non-inferiority to GRAPPA for overall image quality in both readers (p <= .023), though interrater agreement was low (ICC 0.241-0.262), reflecting subjective variability. Secondary exploratory analyses showed heterogeneous preferences. ROI-based CNR was lower for CS (median 169.6; IQR, 91.0-226. vs. 278.2; 181.0-366.2). Aneurysm diameter measurements showed excellent interrater agreement for both techniques (CS ICC, 0.899-0.980; GRAPPA ICC, 0.877-0.973; all p < .001). CONCLUSION CS-accelerated 3D-TOF at 1.5T met non-inferiority criteria vs. GRAPPA-TOF for overall image quality, reducing scan time by 38.7% while preserving aneurysm measurement reliability. However, reduced CNR and reader-preference variability important trade-offs.

title: AI-Based MRI Radiomics for Preoperative Detection of Tumor Deposits in Rectal Cancer: A Bivariate Diagnostic Accuracy Meta-analysis
abstract: Background: In rectal cancer (RC), tumor deposits (TDs) are clinically important as they are associated with a negative impact on prognosis and affect risk stratification as well as management plans. MRI radiomics combined with artificial intelligence (AI) has been explored for non-invasive preoperative TDs detection. However, results vary across studies; therefore, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to pool their diagnostic test accuracy (DTA). Methods: This systematic review and DTA meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Diagnostic Test Accuracy and reported in adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies (PRISMA-DTA). Databases were screened for DTA studies of MRI-based radiomics predicting TDs in adult RC patients with histopathology as reference. Results: Nine studies (2589 patients) were identified. Across included studies, the bivariate meta-analysis showed pooled sensitivity of 0.765 (95% CI 0.714 - 0.809) and specificity of 0.790 (95% CI 0.750 - 0.825), with overall AUC of 0.845 and very low heterogeneity (I2 = 7.3%). In validation datasets, diagnostic performance remained consistent (AUC 0.806), with pooled sensitivity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 - 0.809) and specificity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 - 0.809). For MRI modality, T2 weighted image (T2WI) showed higher sensitivity (0.745) than T2WI plus diffusion weighted image (DWI) (0.697), while T2WI+DWI had higher specificity (0.809 vs 0.737) and AUC (0.829 vs 0.796), with no significant subgroup differences (p[≥]0.192). Models combining radiomics with clinical/radiological variables achieved significantly higher sensitivity (0.842 vs 0.657, p<0.001) and higher AUC (0.827 vs 0.752), with comparable specificity. Conclusion: MRI-based radiomics demonstrates good accuracy for preoperative detection of tumor deposits in RC. The integration of radiomics with clinical or imaging features increases the accuracy of identification. Amongst the MRI modalities, models that utilize the combination of T2WI plus DWI are more accurate than those using T2WI or DWI only.

title: Pathology foundation-model embeddings reveal a morphological landscape of breast lesions beyond diagnostic categories
abstract: Background: Despite rapid advances in computational pathology, including foundation-model embeddings, most approaches remain classifier-based. Breast lesion pathology is an area of unmet clinicopathological need and a compelling setting for morphology-based modeling: diagnostic categories occupy overlapping morphological spectra and reflect heterogeneous pathways of tumor development, thereby posing substantial challenges for pathological diagnosis and subsequent clinical decision-making. However, approaches to delineate morphological continua across diagnostic categories and tumor development remain understudied. Here, we leveraged morphology-based foundation-model embeddings to define a morphologic state space across breast lesion categories and dissect how these embeddings could reflect a pathobiological continuum or sequence associated with tumor development. Methods: To model breast lesion categories in continuous morphology space, we established a leakage-controlled, patient-aware workflow using the frozen foundation model Prov-GigaPath and the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset, a pathologist-annotated hematoxylin-and-eosin (H&E) breast lesion dataset spanning normal tissue, benign proliferative lesions, atypical lesions, ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and invasive carcinoma (IC). Using the BRACS training split, we defined a train-derived principal component analysis (PCA) morphology space. We then performed two complementary analyses: normal-rooted k-nearest-neighbor (kNN)-Dijkstra graph-distance scoring to derive a trajectory-like morphology score without imposing the full ordinal diagnostic sequence; pairwise Energy distance and squared maximum mean discrepancy with a radial-basis-function kernel (RBF-MMD 2 ) to quantify order-free distributional separation among diagnostic categories. Validation and test data were projected into the train-defined reference space to assess reproducibility. Results: Prov-GigaPath embeddings defined a train-derived morphology space with category-associated organization. Without imposing the full diagnostic sequence, normal-rooted kNN-Dijkstra graph distances recovered a trajectory-like morphology arrangement from normal/benign to malignant lesions. Order-free Energy distance and RBF-MMD 2 further supported graded separation among lesion categories. Validation and test datasets preserved the pathological organization. Furthermore, morphological embeddings dissected DCIS heterogeneity associated with concurrent invasive carcinoma, without requiring additional molecular information. Conclusions: Leveraging morphology-based foundation-model embeddings, we defined a morphologic state space across breast lesion categories, allowing nuanced positioning of breast lesions along a pathobiological continuum associated with tumor development. Our approaches pave the way for extracting biologically and clinically relevant information from routine histopathology to guide molecular testing, individualized risk assessment, and cost-efficient clinicopathological decision-making.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning Links Group-Specific Plasma Proteomics to Regional Structural Neuroimaging in Alzheimer's Disease
abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology begins years before clinical symptoms, highlighting the need for scalable biomarkers that capture biological changes across the AD continuum. Broader plasma proteomics may capture systemic processes that vary with disease stage, yet their relationship to AD-related brain neurodegeneration remains unclear. We aimed to identify plasma proteomic signatures across cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD and evaluate their neuroanatomical associations. Methods: We analyzed 146 plasma analytes from 565 Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) participants (58 CN, 396 MCI, 111 AD). Group-specific proteomic signatures were identified using pairwise classification models with nested 5*5 cross-validation. SHAP quantified feature importance, with the top 15 proteins per comparison being prioritized for MRI association analysis. We analyzed 103 regional structural MRI volumes harmonized across 57 acquisition sites using ComBat. Separate ordinary least squares regression tested protein-MRI associations, adjusting for age, sex, APOE4, diagnosis, and intracranial volume, followed by Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Results: Classification models using proteomic data achieved AUC of 0.956 +- 0.017 for CN vs MCI, 0.963 +- 0.011 for MCI vs. AD, and 0.836 +- 0.085 for CN vs. AD. SHAP identified group-dependent proteomic signatures. No protein-MRI associations survived FDR correction for CN vs. MCI. In MCI vs. AD, higher cortisol was associated with lower left precuneus and superior parietal volumes, while higher osteopontin was associated with lower left paracentral and accumbens volumes. In CN vs. AD, higher vitronectin was associated with lower posterior corpus callosum volume. Conclusion: These findings suggest that plasma proteomics capture group-specific systemic biological signals across the AD continuum. Linking ML-prioritized plasma proteins to regional brain structure provides neuroanatomical context for blood-based biomarker discovery.

title: BundleMorphometry: Spatially Resolved White Matter Bundle Shape Analysis Using Nonlinear Streamline-based Registration
abstract: Diffusion MRI tractometry quantifies microstructural properties along white matter (WM) bundles but does not directly measure their geometry, potentially overlooking localized morphological alterations. Here, we introduce BundleMorphometry, a framework for quantifying local WM bundle shape using the analytical Jacobian of nonlinear streamline-based registration. Individual subject bundles are registered to a reference atlas bundle using BundleWarp, a streamline-based nonlinear registration method. We derive the analytical Jacobian of the resulting deformation field and compute its log-determinant (log det J) to quantify local expansion and compression at each streamline point. To enable spatially resolved group comparisons, these measurements are projected onto the two-dimensional grid, capturing variations along and across each bundle. We evaluated BundleMorphometry using two clinical datasets comprising patients with glioma and Parkinson's disease (PD). In the glioma dataset, BundleMorphometry revealed spatially extensive deformation patterns in lesion-affected WM bundles that were not captured by displacement magnitude alone. Additionally, in a group analysis of the PD dataset (32 patients and 32 healthy controls), we identified significant localized morphological differences in the corpus callosum forceps major, mid-body and right spinothalamic tract, with distinct patterns of expansion and compression. These findings demonstrate the potential of BundleMorphometry to advance conventional tractometry by enabling spatially resolved analysis of bundle morphology.

title: Generalizable virtual staining from histopathology to spatial proteomics across biological scales
abstract: Large histology archives capture morphological correlates of molecular tissue states but lack direct spatial protein measurements. In this study, we show that routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histology can provide a queryable, morphology-based representation of spatial protein expression that remains informative from pixels to patients. To achieve this, we developed QUEST, a model framework that represents protein markers as semantic queries for flexible multiplex immunofluorescence (MIF) prediction. Trained on a heterogeneous atlas of paired H&E and MIF images comprising over 10,000 tissue regions, QUEST captured morphological patterns associated with protein markers and reconstructed their expression intensities across diverse tissue types and cohorts. Its utility extended beyond image reconstruction and preserved biologically meaningful information across multiple scales: virtual staining preserved protein marker expression at the cellular and tissue scales, supported cell phenotyping, cellular neighborhood analysis, and characterization of spatial tissue organization, retained clinically relevant signals for patient stratification, and enabled H&E-based queries to retrieve MIF references with similar molecular profiles. These findings position virtual staining not simply as image generation but as a flexible interface between routine histology and spatial proteomics, expanding the analytical value of existing H&E archives.

title: RyR2-Mediated Ca2+ Leak Drives Progressive Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathy
abstract: Background: Abnormal sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca2+ release through ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) is a well-established mechanism of ventricular arrhythmias. Whether persistent RyR2 dysfunction can also initiate the structural remodeling characteristic of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) remains unknown. We tested the hypothesis that chronic RyR2-mediated Ca2+ leak is sufficient to couple electrical instability to progressive cardiomyopathy. Methods We generated a rabbit carrying the severe gain-of-function RyR2-V2475F mutation and characterized disease progression using longitudinal cardiac phenotyping, continuous electrocardiographic monitoring, cellular electrophysiology and Ca2+ imaging, histopathology, biochemical analyses, and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). Therapeutic potential was evaluated by continuous treatment with the selective RyR2 inhibitor ent-verticilide for two months. Results RyR2-V2475F rabbits developed spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and progressive right ventricular (RV)-dominant fibrofatty cardiomyopathy recapitulating major features of human ACM. Malignant ventricular arrhythmias preceded overt structural remodeling and were associated at the cellular level with early spontaneous Ca2+ release and early afterdepolarizations. Early disease was characterized by remodeling of excitation-contraction coupling with preserved SR Ca2+ load and contractile function despite RyR2 dysfunction; upon disease progression, these compensatory changes were accompanied by SR Ca2+ depletion, impaired RV contractility and reduced left ventricular filling. Single-nucleus transcriptomics identified early fibroblast expansion and predicted cardiomyocyte-centered paracrine signaling before advanced fibrofatty infiltration. Cardiomyocytes also exhibited an altered lipid-metabolic transcriptome and intracellular lipid accumulation, accompanied by enhanced mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake. Selective RyR2 inhibition markedly reduced ventricular tachycardia burden and preserved RV contraction and LV filling during disease progression. Conclusions Severe RyR2 gain-of-function can lead to both malignant ventricular arrhythmias and progressive arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in a large-animal model, establishing persistent intracellular Ca2+ dysregulation as a mechanistic link between electrical and structural heart disease. The ability of selective RyR2 inhibition to suppress arrhythmias and preserve cardiac function identifies RyR2 as a potentially actionable therapeutic target in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

title: Peripheral immune biomarkers, brain imaging phenotypes and treatment response in major depressive disorder
abstract: Immune dysregulation is implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), but its links to clinical features and in vivo brain phenotypes remain uncertain. We examined ten plasma biomarkers in 36 unmedicated MDD patients and 48 control participants using high-sensitivity immune profiling at baseline, alongside PET/MR imaging of brain serotonin transporter (SERT) binding and regional structural measures. Patients underwent three months of antidepressant treatment and were followed up with MR imaging. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) was higher in MDD patients (β = 0.66, 95% CI 0.22 - 1.11), and interleukin-33 (IL-33) correlated with subcortical volumes across all participants (β = 0.22, 95% CI 0.07 - 0.38). No marker correlated with SERT binding or cortical thickness after correction, and neither SERT binding nor brain structural measures differed by diagnosis. In the longitudinal analysis, interleukin-13 (IL-13) was associated with greater antidepressant response during first-line treatment with escitalopram (β = 1.09, 95% CI 0.56 - 1.61). IL-15 and IL-13 showed nominal associations with hippocampal volume increase after treatment. These findings suggest astroglial involvement in MDD and that peripheral immune states relate to subcortical brain structure. IL-13 is a candidate prognostic marker of response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Its tentative association with longitudinal changes in hippocampal volume suggests that immune processes in MDD may be related to both the capacity for clinical improvement and brain structural plasticity during treatment.

title: Investigating AI's potential in risk-stratifying lung cancer screenings for extending screening intervals and reducing workload: A retrospective analysis of a tertiary hospital cohort
abstract: Objective: We aimed to 1) evaluate whether AI algorithms could identify a very low-risk sub-population Lung-RADS 1/2 cases suitable for a safe switch to biennial screening, and 2) externally validate Sybil, an imaging-based deep learning lung cancer risk prediction tool. Materials and methods: We gathered all lung cancer screenings (LCSs) from a tertiary safety-net hospital (n=3120, up to September 2024), manually extracted relevant clinical data, and analyzed Sybil's performance across various subgroups, with a specific focus on Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases. We simulated LCS interval extension using Sybil and the Brock model risk scores calibrated on a subset of the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST). Confidence intervals were obtained through bootstrapping. Results: The median follow-up was 2.3 years (interquartile range 1.5-3.1), with a total 6-year cancer incidence rate of 2.3% (72/3120). Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases comprised 90.5% of our scans. Sybil's overall area under the curve (AUC) ranged from 0.819 to 0.912; while its 2-year AUC for Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases was 0.746. In the screening interval extension simulation, calibrating for a 30% shift to biennial screening translated into 33.8% of negative screens in our data being safely extended using Sybil, with no delayed cancers. The Brock model demonstrated an AUC of 0.513 on our data, with a sensitivity of 18.2% using the 1.5% threshold. Conclusion: Sybil has the potential to safely extend LCS intervals for low-risk individuals, reducing radiology workload and opening spots for life-saving new screenings.

title: Olfactory Function in Preclinical Alzheimer's Disease: A Multi-Cohort Study
abstract: Introduction: Olfactory impairment is an early feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, it is unclear if olfactory performance reflects early pathological changes during preclinical AD and/or predicts subsequent clinical progression among characterized cognitively normal (CN) individuals. We aimed to determine whether odor identification differs by amyloid status, relates to medial temporal lobe (MTL) tau burden and morphometry, and predicts longitudinal conversion to mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Methods: We analyzed data from 257 cognitively normal (CN) older adults enrolled in PREVENT-AD (n = 217) and UCLouvain (n = 40), including 76 amyloid-positive (CN A+) and 181 amyloid-negative participants (CN A−). Participants completed olfactory testing, underwent tau-PET imaging, and structural MRI. Results: CN A+ participants had significantly lower odor identification performance than CN A− participants, with no evidence of cohort heterogeneity. Tau-PET associations with odor identification differed by cohort. After whole-brain FDR correction and exclusion of extreme values, parahippocampal tau burden was negatively associated with odor identification score in UCLouvain ([18F]MK-6240), an association that was not found in PREVENT-AD ([18F]flortaucipir). No morphometric association survived multiple comparison correction. In 250 participants with longitudinal follow-up, each 10-percentage-point higher odor identification score was associated with a 16% lower hazard of incident MCI, independent of baseline global cognition and APOE ϵ4-carrier status. Discussion: Odor identification was lower in preclinical AD and associated with incident MCI independently of baseline global cognition and APOE ϵ4-carrier status. Its association with parahippocampal tau burden differed between cohorts, supporting further investigation using harmonized imaging methods.

title: Rapid Detection and Initial Treatment of Life-Threatening Subdural Hematoma in a Sheep Model
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause of death and disability in people under 40 worldwide. There is an unmet need for detection and treatment of life-threatening TBI when computed tomography (CT) scanners and neurosurgeons are unavailable. We developed a new handheld frequency-domain multidetector infrared hemorrhage detection device. Using the new device, military pre-hospital medics required <4 minutes to detect life-threatening subdural hematoma in a sheep model. We developed a second device that allows non-neurosurgeons to safely create a burr hole and partially remove clotted subdural blood. In sheep, the treatment device reduced intracranial pressure within 20 minutes, and improved post-anesthesia blinded neurological outcomes. With human use adaptation, these devices could allow rapid detection and initial treatment of some life-threatening TBIs in challenging situations.

title: Late radiation-induced brain injury is associated with functional cerebrovascular impairment without structural vessel loss in mice
abstract: Background: Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) is a major and often irreversible complication of cranial radiotherapy, affecting up to 90% of long-term survivors. Although cerebrovascular damage is a leading mechanistic hypothesis, whether chronic resting hypoperfusion occurs independently of structural vessel loss remains unknown. The aim of this study was to comprehensively characterize cerebrovascular, structural, and behavioral outcomes in a murine model of late RIBI to determine the primary drivers of vascular dysfunction. Methods: Adult C57BL/6 mice underwent 12 Gy whole-brain irradiation and were assessed one year later using laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI), 7T MRI, immunohistochemistry, and behavioral testing. Results: Irradiated mice exhibited reduced pial flow velocity and flow area by LSCI, indicative of upstream cerebrovascular dysfunction, while bulk cortical tissue perfusion was preserved. This pial hypoperfusion was accompanied by cerebral atrophy, decreased T2* relaxation time and tissue iron deposition consistent with chronic microhemorrhage across multiple brain regions by MRI, blood-brain barrier disruption reflected by reduced ZO-1 and VE-cadherin expression, and increased anxiety-like behavior. Strikingly, capillary density, pericyte coverage, astrocyte endfeet, and NeuN-positive neuronal nuclei were all preserved. Conclusion: These findings demonstrate that functional vascular impairment - not structural vessel or neuronal loss - drives hypoperfusion and blood-brain barrier disruption in late RIBI. This dissociation between vascular dysfunction and rarefaction reframes the pathophysiology of RIBI and identifies endothelial dysfunction as a tractable therapeutic target for intervention.

The aim of this study was to comprehensively characterize cerebrovascular, structural, and behavioral outcomes in a murine model of late RIBI to determine the primary drivers of vascular dysfunction.

Methods:

Adult C57BL/6 mice underwent 12 Gy whole-brain irradiation and were assessed one year later using laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI), 7T MRI, immunohistochemistry, and behavioral testing.

Results:

Irradiated mice exhibited reduced pial flow velocity and flow area by LSCI, indicative of upstream cerebrovascular dysfunction, while bulk cortical tissue perfusion was preserved. This pial hypoperfusion was accompanied by cerebral atrophy, decreased T2* relaxation time and tissue iron deposition consistent with chronic microhemorrhage across multiple brain regions by MRI, blood-brain barrier disruption reflected by reduced ZO-1 and VE-cadherin expression, and increased anxiety-like behavior. Strikingly, capillary density, pericyte coverage, astrocyte endfeet, and NeuN-positive neuronal nuclei were all preserved.

Conclusion:

These findings demonstrate that functional vascular impairment - not structural vessel or neuronal loss - drives hypoperfusion and blood-brain barrier disruption in late RIBI. This dissociation between vascular dysfunction and rarefaction reframes the pathophysiology of RIBI and identifies endothelial dysfunction as a tractable therapeutic target for intervention.

title: Cross-cancer knowledge transfer for lymph node metastasis prediction: Applicability of an axillary lymph node-based deep learning model
abstract: Evaluation of lymph node (LN) metastasis is critical for cancer staging and treatment planning. Since radiologic hallmarks of metastatic LNs are shared across primary cancers, a computed tomography (CT)-based deep learning (DL) classifier developed from one anatomy may transfer to others. This study built a DenseNet-121 ensemble model using clinical-implication-applied preprocessing and evaluated its cross-anatomical generalizability to LNs from diverse primary cancers. A DenseNet-121 ensemble model combining fixed-size cropping (FSC) and adjustable square cropping (ASC) was trained from ImageNet initialization on an axillary lymph node (ALN) dataset (n = 1,128 from 523 breast cancer patients). The model utilized clinical-implication-applied perinodal cropping with bicubic filtering and standardized resizing. To test cross-anatomical generalizability, an external dataset of 256 CT images across four anatomical regions was evaluated: cervical, mediastinal, upper-abdominal, and lower-abdominal LNs. Perinodal free margins were systematically varied from 10% to 40% to optimize the balance between context preservation and surround interference. Bicubic filtering and standardized resizing yielded the highest internal performance on the original ALN dataset (FSC-ASC ensemble area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.958, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.920–0.987 at 40% margin). The model demonstrated site-dependent, above-chance generalizability across all external regions. Cervical LNs achieved the highest performance at a 40% margin (AUROC 0.939, 95% CI 0.875–0.989). Mediastinal LNs peaked at a 10% margin (AUROC 0.796, 95% CI 0.672–0.903), with wider margins degrading performance due to adjacent structural interference. Upper-abdominal and lower-abdominal LNs reached optimal performance at a 30% margin (AUROC 0.814 for upper; AUROC 0.917 for lower). A single ALN-trained DL model can accurately predict LN metastasis across cervical, mediastinal, and abdominal stations through site-specific perinodal margin tuning. These findings support the feasibility of cross-cancer knowledge transfer and the clinical utility of generalizable backbones for pan-cancer nodal assessment.

title: Artificial Intelligence Versus Human Interpretation in Diagnostic Radiology: A Systematic Review of Diagnostic Accuracy and Operational Efficiency.
abstract: Rising imaging workload and a shortage of radiology specialists have driven interest in artificial intelligence (AI) to improve diagnostic speed and accuracy. This systematic review, without meta-analysis, describes how AI affects diagnostic accuracy and operational efficiency compared with human interpretation in diagnostic radiology. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) and Cochrane guidance, PubMed, ClinicalKey, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar were searched on 11 April 2026 for studies published from January 2019 onwards. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and a Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2)-based risk-of-bias assessment. Twenty-one studies were included: 11 compared standalone AI with human readers, six compared AI-assisted with unassisted readers, and four reported both; 18 evaluated task-specific image-analysis AI and three evaluated generative AI models. Because no subgroup was homogeneous enough to pool, we synthesised results narratively and stratified them by comparison type, AI category, imaging modality, and study quality. Standalone image-analysis AI achieved high sensitivity for fractures and selected chest findings but performed less well on subtle findings and lower-quality images, and in one computed tomography-referenced comparison a radiologist outperformed AI. AI assistance improved reader performance more consistently, particularly among less experienced readers. Generative models did not reach specialist performance on complex tasks. Efficiency gains were concentrated in normal studies, and the only randomised trial found lower mammography screen-reading workload with similar early screening performance. No study assessed patient outcomes, and 18 of 21 studies were retrospective. This evidence supports AI only as a supervised, complementary tool; improvements in diagnostic accuracy should not be equated with clinical benefit.

title: From Spiradenocarcinoma to Spiradenoma: A Case of Histopathological Diagnostic Reclassification.
abstract: Spiradenocarcinoma is a rare malignant cutaneous adnexal neoplasm that may arise from a preexisting spiradenoma. Distinguishing benign from malignant lesions can be challenging, and diagnostic classification has important implications for treatment and follow-up. A 37-year-old woman presented with an approximately 3-cm erythematous-violaceous nodule on the right ankle that had been present for five years and had recently grown rapidly. The initial histopathological assessment described a malignant epithelial neoplasm compatible with spiradenocarcinoma associated with a benign spiradenoma component. The patient underwent wider surgical re-excision with clinical margins exceeding 1 cm, and computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no metastatic disease. No residual neoplasm was identified in the re-excision specimen. Subsequent review of the original histological slides at a second laboratory identified a well-circumscribed, lobulated, solid-cystic dermal lesion with two distinct epithelial cell populations and an interspersed lymphocytic infiltrate, without infiltrative growth, nuclear atypia, mitotic activity, or necrosis in the reviewed material. The diagnosis was revised to benign spiradenoma. Immunohistochemistry supported the diagnosis of an eccrine neoplasm. This case illustrates the diagnostic challenges in distinguishing spiradenoma from spiradenocarcinoma and the clinical implications of discrepant histopathological assessments. Morphological evaluation remains central to classification, while immunohistochemistry provides complementary information.
